nodes.name: simplex category
nodes.statement: 1.1.1. Notation (the simplex category). Let $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ denote the simplex category of finite nonempty ordinals $[n]=\{0<1<\cdots<n\}$ and order-preserving maps.
differentia: finite nonempty ordinals $[n]=\{0<1<\cdots<n\}$ and order-preserving maps

nodes.name: elementary face and degeneracy operators
nodes.statement: These include in particular the $$ \begin{array}{ccc} \text { elementary face operators } & {[n-1] \stackrel{\delta^{i}}{\rightarrow}[n]} & 0 \leq i \leq n \\ \text { elementary degeneracy operators } & {[n+1] \xrightarrow{\sigma^{i}}[n]} & 0 \leq i \leq n \end{array} $$ whose images, respectively, omit and double up on the element $i \in[n]$.
nodes.statement_short: The elementary face maps $\delta^i:[n-1]\to[n]$ and degeneracy maps $\sigma^i:[n+1]\to[n]$ omit, resp. double, the element $i$.

nodes.name: epi-mono factorization in the simplex category
nodes.statement: Every morphism in $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ factors uniquely as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism; these epimorphisms, the degeneracy operators, decompose as composites of elementary degeneracy operators, while the monomorphisms, the face operators, decompose as composites of elementary face operators.
conclusions: Every morphism in $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ factors uniquely as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Every simplicial operator factors uniquely as a degeneracy followed by a face operator, each a composite of elementary ones.

nodes.name: simplicial sets
nodes.statement: The category of simplicial sets is the category s et $:=$ Set ${ }^{\Delta^{\text {op }}}$ of presheaves on the simplex category.

nodes.name: standard simplex, horn and boundary
nodes.statement: We write $\Delta[n]$ for the standard $n$-simplex the simplicial set represented by $[n] \in \Delta$, and $\Lambda^{k}[n] \subset$ $\partial \Delta[n] \subset \Delta[n]$ for its $k$-horn and boundary sphere, respectively. The sphere $\partial \Delta[n]$ is the simplicial subset generated by the codimension-one faces of the $n$-simplex, while the horn $\Lambda^{k}[n]$ is the further simplicial subset that omits the face opposite the vertex $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for the standard $n$-simplex $\Delta[n]$, its boundary sphere and its $k$-horn $\Lambda^k[n]$.

nodes.name: n-simplices of a simplicial set
nodes.statement: Given a simplicial set $X$, it is conventional to write $X_{n}$ for the set of $n$-simplices, defined by evaluating at $[n] \in \boldsymbol{\Delta}$.

nodes.name: face of a simplex
nodes.statement: Accordingly, we write $x \cdot \delta^{i}$ for the $i$ th face of the $n$-simplex, an $(n-1)$-simplex classified by the composite map $$ \Delta[n-1] \xrightarrow{\delta^{i}} \Delta[n] \xrightarrow{x} X . $$

nodes.name: quasi-category
nodes.statement: 1.1.2. Definition (quasi-category). A quasi-category is a simplicial set $A$ in which any inner horn can be extended to a simplex, solving the displayed lifting problem:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-02_198_731_1579_703} (1.1.3)
differentia: any inner horn can be extended to a simplex

nodes.name: Kan complex
nodes.statement: Quasi-categories were first introduced by Boardman and Vogt [21] under the name "weak Kan complexes," a Kan complex being a simplicial set admitting extensions as in (1.1.3) along all horn inclusions $n \geq 1,0 \leq k \leq n$.
differentia: admitting extensions as in (1.1.3) along all horn inclusions

nodes.name: nerve
nodes.statement: 1.1.4. Definition (nerve). The category $\boldsymbol{C} a t$ of 1 -categories embeds fully faithfully into the category of simplicial sets via the nerve functor. An $n$-simplex in the nerve of a 1 -category $C$ is a sequence of $n$ composable arrows in $C$, or equally a functor $\mathrm{m}+\mathbb{1} \rightarrow C$ from the ordinal category $\mathrm{m}+\mathbb{1}:=[n]$ with objects $0, \ldots, n$ and a unique arrow $i \rightarrow j$ just when $i \leq j$.
nodes.statement_short: The nerve of a category $C$ has as $n$-simplices the strings of $n$ composable arrows, i.e. functors $[n]\to C$.

nodes.name: nerves are 2-coskeletal
nodes.statement: 1.1.5. Remark. The nerve of a category $C$ is 2-coskeletal as a simplicial set, meaning that every sphere $\partial \Delta[n] \rightarrow C$ with $n \geq 3$ is filled uniquely by an $n$-simplex in $C$ (see Definition C.5.2). Note a sphere $\partial \Delta[2] \rightarrow C$ extends to a 2-simplex if and only if that arrow along its diagonal edge is the composite of the arrows along the edges in the inner horn $\Lambda^{1}[2] \subset \partial \Delta[2] \rightarrow C$. The simplices in dimension 3 and above witness the associativity of the composition of the path of composable arrows found along their spine, the 1-skeletal simplicial subset formed by the edges connecting adjacent vertices. In fact, as suggested by the proof of Proposition 1.1.6, any simplicial set in which inner horns admit unique fillers is isomorphic to the nerve of a 1-category (see Exercise 1.1.iv).
nodes.statement_short: Nerves are 2-coskeletal: 2-simplices witness composition, higher simplices associativity; unique inner horn fillers characterize nerves.

nodes.name: ordinal notation for standard simplices
nodes.statement: For instance, the standard simplex $\Delta[n]$ is isomorphic to the nerve of the ordinal category $\mathrm{m}+1$, and we frequently adopt the latter notation - writing $\mathbb{1}:=\Delta[0], 2:=\Delta[1], 3:=\Delta[2]$, and so on - to suggest the correct categorical intuition.

nodes.name: nerves are quasi-categories
nodes.statement: 1.1.6. Proposition (nerves are quasi-categories). Nerves of categories are quasi-categories.
conclusions: Nerves of categories are quasi-categories.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.1.6
nodes.statement: Proof. Via the isomorphism $C \cong \operatorname{cosk}_{2} C$ from Remark 1.1.5 and the adjunction $\operatorname{sk}_{2} \dashv \operatorname{cosk}_{2}$ of C.5.2, the required lifting problem displayed below-left transposes to the one displayed below-right:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-03_203_1027_1504_548}\\ The functor $\mathrm{sk}_{2}$ replaces a simplicial set by its 2-skeleton, the simplicial subset generated by the simplices of dimension at most two. For $n \geq 4$, the inclusion $\operatorname{sk}_{2} \Lambda^{k}[n] \hookrightarrow \operatorname{sk}_{2} \Delta[n]$ is an isomorphism, in which case the lifting problems on the right admit (unique) solutions. So it remains only to solve the lifting problems on the left in the cases $n=2$ and $n=3$. To that end consider\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-03_196_1035_1991_544}\\ An inner horn $\Lambda^{1}[2] \rightarrow C$ defines a composable pair of arrows in $C$; an extension to a 2 -simplex exists precisely because any composable pair of arrows admits a (unique) composite. An inner horn $\Lambda^{1}[3] \rightarrow C$ specifies the data of three composable arrows in $C$, as displayed in the following diagram, together with the composites $g f, h g$, and $(h g) f$.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-04_304_372_373_874}\\ Because composition is associative, the arrow $(h g) f$ is also the composite of $g f$ followed by $h$, which proves that the 2 -simplex opposite the vertex $c_{1}$ is present in $C$; by 2-coskeletality, the 3 -simplex filling this boundary sphere is also present in $C$. The filler for a horn $\Lambda^{2}[3] \rightarrow C$ is constructed similarly.
nodes.statement_short: By 2-coskeletality reduce to inner horns of dimension 2 and 3; these are filled by composition and associativity in $C$.

nodes.name: homotopy relation on 1-simplices
nodes.statement: 1.1.7. Definition (homotopy relation on 1 -simplices). A parallel pair of 1 -simplices $f, g$ in a simplicial set $X$ are homotopic if there exists a 2-simplex whose boundary takes either of the following forms ${ }^{2}$\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-04_151_239_986_763}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-04_151_237_986_1122} (1.1.8)\\ or if $f$ and $g$ are in the same equivalence class generated by this relation.

nodes.name: homotopic 1-simplices in a quasi-category
nodes.statement: 1.1.9. Lemma (homotopic 1-simplices in a quasi-category). Parallel 1-simplices $f$ and $g$ in a quasi-category are homotopic if and only if there exists a 2-simplex of any or equivalently all of the forms displayed in (1.1.8).
also_stated_at: In a quasi-category, the relation witnessed by either of the types of 2-simplex on display in (1.1.8) is an equivalence relation and these equivalence relations coincide.
conclusions: are homotopic if and only if there exists a 2-simplex of any or equivalently all of the forms displayed in (1.1.8).
equivalent_conditions: there exists a 2-simplex of any or equivalently all of the forms displayed in (1.1.8).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1.9
nodes.statement: Proof. Exercise 1.1.ii.
nodes.statement_short: Deferred to Exercise 1.1.ii.

nodes.name: homotopy category of a simplicial set
nodes.statement: 1.1.10. Definition (the homotopy category [44, §2.4]). By 1-truncating, any simplicial set $X$ has an underlying reflexive directed graph with the 0 -simplices of $X$ defining the objects and the 1 -simplices defining the arrows: $$ X_{1} \xrightarrow[\cdot \delta^{0}]{\xrightarrow{\stackrel{\cdot \delta^{1}}{\leftarrow \cdot \sigma^{0}}-}} X_{0}, $$ By convention, the source of an arrow $f \in X_{1}$ is its 0th face $f \cdot \delta^{1}$ (the face opposite 1) while the target is its 1st face $f \cdot \delta^{0}$ (the face opposite 0). The free category on this reflexive directed graph has $X_{0}$ as its object set, degenerate 1 -simplices serving as identity morphisms, and nonidentity morphisms defined to be finite directed paths of nondegenerate 1-simplices. The homotopy category $\mathrm{h} X$ of $X$ is the quotient of the free category on its underlying reflexive directed graph by the congruence ${ }^{3}$ generated by imposing a composition relation $h=g \circ f$ witnessed by 2-simplices\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-04_146_285_2144_918}
nodes.genus: quotient of the free category on its underlying reflexive directed graph
nodes.statement_short: The homotopy category $hX$: free category on the 1-skeleton of $X$ modulo the composition relations witnessed by 2-simplices.

nodes.name: homotopy category of a nerve
nodes.statement: The homotopy category of the nerve of a 1-category is isomorphic to the original category, as the 2-simplices in the nerve witness all of the composition relations satisfied by the arrows in the underlying reflexive directed graph.
conclusions: The homotopy category of the nerve of a 1-category is isomorphic to the original category

nodes.name: homotopy category is left adjoint to the nerve
nodes.statement: 1.1.11. Proposition. The nerve embedding admits a left adjoint, namely the functor which sends a simplicial set to its homotopy category:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-05_118_382_697_870}
conclusions: The nerve embedding admits a left adjoint, namely the functor which sends a simplicial set to its homotopy category:

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.1.11
nodes.statement: Proof. For any simplicial set $X$, there is a natural map from $X$ to the nerve of its homotopy category $\mathrm{h} X$; since nerves are 2 -coskeletal, it suffices to define the map $\mathrm{sk}_{2} X \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} X$, and this is given immediately by the construction of Definition 1.1.10. Note that the quotient map $X \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} X$ becomes an isomorphism upon applying the homotopy category functor and is already an isomorphism whenever $X$ is the nerve of a category. Thus the adjointness follows from Lemma B.4.2 or by direct verification of the triangle equalities.
nodes.statement_short: Build the unit $X\to hX$ on the 2-skeleton via Definition 1.1.10; adjointness from Lemma B.4.2 or the triangle identities.

nodes.name: the homotopy category of a quasi-category
nodes.statement: 1.1.12. Lemma (the homotopy category of a quasi-category). If $A$ is a quasi-category then its homotopy category $\mathrm{h} A$ has \begin{itemize} \item[-] the set of 0 -simplices $A_{0}$ as its objects \item[-] the set of homotopy classes of 1 -simplices $A_{1}$ as its arrows \item[-] the identity arrow at $a \in A_{0}$ represented by the degenerate 1-simplex $a \cdot \sigma^{0} \in A_{1}$ \item[-] a composition relation $h=g \circ f$ in $\mathrm{h} A$ between the homotopy classes of arrows represented by any given 1 -simplices $f, g, h \in A_{1}$ if and only if there exists a 2 -simplex with boundary \end{itemize}
conclusions: its homotopy category $\mathrm{h} A$ has
nodes.statement_short: For a quasi-category $A$, $hA$ has objects $A_0$, arrows homotopy classes of 1-simplices, composition witnessed by single 2-simplices.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1.12
nodes.statement: Proof. Exercise 1.1.iii.
nodes.statement_short: Deferred to Exercise 1.1.iii.

nodes.name: isomorphism in a quasi-category
nodes.statement: 1.1.13. Definition (isomorphism in a quasi-category). A 1-simplex in a quasi-category is an isomorph$\mathbf{i s m}^{4}$ just when it represents an isomorphism in the homotopy category. By Lemma 1.1.12 this means that $f: a \rightarrow b$ is an isomorphism if and only if there exists a 1 -simplex $f^{-1}: b \rightarrow a$ together with a pair of 2-simplices\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-05_139_234_2178_768}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-05_130_232_2187_1122}
differentia: it represents an isomorphism in the homotopy category

nodes.name: special outer horn filling
nodes.statement: 1.1.14. Proposition (special outer horn filling). Any quasi-category $A$ admits fillers for those outer horns\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-06_205_1013_1167_563}\\ in which the edges $\left.g\right|_{\{0,1\}}$ and $\left.h\right|_{\{n-1, n\}}$ are isomorphisms.
assumptions: in which the edges $\left.g\right|_{\{0,1\}}$ and $\left.h\right|_{\{n-1, n\}}$ are isomorphisms.
conclusions: Any quasi-category $A$ admits fillers for those outer horns

nodes.name: Kan complexes are quasi-categories with groupoidal homotopy category
nodes.statement: 1.1.15. Corollary. A quasi-category is a Kan complex if and only if its homotopy category is a groupoid.
conclusions: A quasi-category is a Kan complex if and only if its homotopy category is a groupoid.
equivalent_conditions: A quasi-category is a Kan complex
its homotopy category is a groupoid.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.1.15
nodes.statement: Proof. If the homotopy category of a quasi-category is a groupoid, then all of its 1-simplices are isomorphisms, and Proposition 1.1.14 then implies that all inner and outer horns have fillers. Thus, the quasi-category is a Kan complex. Conversely, in a Kan complex, all outer horns can be filled and in particular fillers for the horns displayed in Definition 1.1.13 can be used to construct left and right inverses for any 1-simplex, which can be rectified to a single two-sided inverse by Lemma 1.1.12.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions: special outer horn filling (Prop. 1.1.14) gives all horn fillers; conversely outer horn fillers build inverses.

nodes.name: maximal sub Kan complex
nodes.statement: A quasi-category contains $A$ a canonical maximal sub Kan complex $A^{\simeq}$, the simplicial subset spanned by those 1-simplices that are isomorphisms.
differentia: spanned by those 1-simplices that are isomorphisms

nodes.name: homotopy coherent isomorphism
nodes.statement: Just as the arrows in a quasi-category $A$ are represented by simplicial maps $2 \rightarrow A$ whose domain is the nerve of the free-living arrow, the isomorphisms in a quasi-category can be represented by diagrams $\mathbb{I} \rightarrow A$ whose domain, called the homotopy coherent isomorphism, is the nerve of the free-living isomorphism:

nodes.name: isomorphisms extend to homotopy coherent isomorphisms
nodes.statement: 1.1.16. Corollary. An arrow $f$ in a quasi-category $A$ is an isomorphism if and only if it extends to a homotopy coherent isomorphism\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-07_193_197_350_963}
conclusions: is an isomorphism if and only if it extends to a homotopy coherent isomorphism
equivalent_conditions: it extends to a homotopy coherent isomorphism

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.1.16
nodes.statement: Proof. If $f$ is an isomorphism, the map $f: 2 \rightarrow A$ lands in the maximal sub Kan complex contained in $A$ :\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-07_193_301_667_911}\\ By Exercise 1.1.v, the inclusion 2 ↪ II can be expressed as a sequential composite of pushouts of outer horn inclusions. Since $A^{\simeq}$ is a Kan complex, this shows that the required extension exists and in fact lands in $A^{\simeq} \subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: An isomorphism lands in the maximal sub Kan complex; $2\hookrightarrow\mathbb{I}$ is built from outer horns, which a Kan complex fills.

nodes.name: exponential of simplicial sets
nodes.statement: By the Yoneda lemma and the defining adjunction, an $n$-simplex in the exponential $Y^{X}$ corresponds to a simplicial map $X \times \Delta[n] \rightarrow Y$, and its faces and degeneracies are computed by precomposing in the simplex variable.

nodes.name: isofibration
nodes.statement: 1.1.17. Definition (isofibration). A simplicial map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories is an isofibration if it lifts against the inner horn inclusions, as displayed below-left, and also against the inclusion of either vertex into the free-living isomorphism II.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-07_194_278_1587_717}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-07_184_206_1594_1208}\\ To notationally distinguish the isofibrations, we depict them as arrows "→" with two heads.
nodes.genus: simplicial map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories
differentia: it lifts against the inner horn inclusions
also against the inclusion of either vertex into the free-living isomorphism II.

nodes.name: special outer horn lifting
nodes.statement: 1.1.18. Proposition (special outer horn lifting). Any isofibration between quasi-categories $f: A \rightarrow B$ admits lifts against those outer horns\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-07_214_279_2076_562}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-07_214_520_2076_1054}\\ in which the edges $\left.g\right|_{\{0,1\}},\left.h\right|_{\{n-1, n\}},\left.k\right|_{\{0,1\}}$, and $\left.\ell\right|_{\{n-1, n\}}$ are isomorphisms.
assumptions: in which the edges $\left.g\right|_{\{0,1\}},\left.h\right|_{\{n-1, n\}},\left.k\right|_{\{0,1\}}$, and $\left.\ell\right|_{\{n-1, n\}}$ are isomorphisms.
conclusions: Any isofibration between quasi-categories $f: A \rightarrow B$ admits lifts against those outer horns

nodes.name: basic properties of isofibrations
nodes.statement: 1.1.19. Observation. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] For any simplicial set $X$, the unique map $X \rightarrow 1$ whose codomain is the terminal simplicial set is an isofibration if and only if $X$ is a quasi-category. \item[(ii)] Any collection of maps, such as the isofibrations, that is characterized by a right lifting property is automatically closed under composition, product, pullback, retract, and (inverse) limits of towers (see Lemma C.2.3). \item[(iii)] Combining (i) and (ii), if $A \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration, and $B$ is a quasi-category, then so is $A$. \item[(iv)] The isofibrations generalize the eponymous categorical notion. The nerve of any functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ between categories defines a map of simplicial sets that lifts against the inner horn inclusions. This map then defines an isofibration if and only if given any isomorphism in $B$ and specified object in $A$ lifting either its domain or codomain, there exists an isomorphism in $A$ with that domain or codomain lifting the isomorphism in $B$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: the unique map $X \rightarrow 1$ whose codomain is the terminal simplicial set is an isofibration if and only if $X$ is a quasi-category.
is automatically closed under composition, product, pullback, retract, and (inverse) limits of towers (see Lemma C.2.3).
if $A \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration, and $B$ is a quasi-category, then so is $A$.
nodes.statement_short: $X\to 1$ is an isofibration iff $X$ is a quasi-category; isofibrations are closed under limits; they generalize isofibrations of categories.

nodes.name: Leibniz exponential stability of isofibrations
nodes.statement: 1.1.20. Proposition. If $i: X \hookrightarrow Y$ is a monomorphism and $f: A \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration, then the induced Leibniz exponential map $i \widehat{\hbar} f$\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-08_352_447_1038_842} (1.1.21)\\ is again an isofibration.
conclusions: the induced Leibniz exponential map $i \widehat{\hbar} f$

nodes.name: quasi-categories form an exponential ideal
nodes.statement: 1.1.22. Corollary. If $X$ is a simplicial set and $A$ is a quasi-category, then $A^{X}$ is a quasi-category. Moreover, a 1-simplex in $A^{X}$ is an isomorphism if and only if its components at each vertex of $X$ are isomorphisms in $A$.
also_stated_at: Our next aim is to show that the quasi-categories define an exponential ideal in the simplicially enriched category of simplicial sets: if $X$ is a simplicial set and $A$ is a quasi-category, then $A^{X}$ is a quasi-category.
conclusions: $A^{X}$ is a quasi-category.
a 1-simplex in $A^{X}$ is an isomorphism if and only if its components at each vertex of $X$ are isomorphisms in $A$.
$A^{X}$ is a quasi-category.
a 1-simplex in $A^{X}$ is an isomorphism if and only if its components at each vertex of $X$ are isomorphisms in $A$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.1.22
nodes.statement: Proof. The first statement is a special case of Proposition 1.1.20 (see Exercise 1.1.vii), while the second statement is proven similarly by arguing with marked simplicial sets (see Corollary D.4.19).
nodes.statement_short: First part specializes Proposition 1.1.20; second via marked simplicial sets (Corollary D.4.19).

nodes.name: equivalence of quasi-categories
nodes.statement: 1.1.23. Definition (equivalences of quasi-categories). A map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories is an equivalence if it extends to the data of a "homotopy equivalence" with the free-living isomorphism II serving as the interval: that is, if there exist maps $g: B \rightarrow A$,\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-08_315_245_1878_680}\\ and\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-08_311_235_1879_1214}\\ We write "→" to decorate equivalences and $A \simeq B$ to indicate the presence of an equivalence $A \xrightarrow{3}$.
nodes.genus: A map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories
nodes.statement_short: An equivalence of quasi-categories is a homotopy equivalence using the homotopy coherent isomorphism $\mathbb{I}$ as interval.

nodes.name: equivalences of quasi-categories induce equivalences of homotopy categories
nodes.statement: 1.1.24. Remark. If $f: A \rightarrow B$ is an equivalence of quasi-categories, then the functor $\mathrm{h} f: \mathrm{h} A \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} B$ is an equivalence of categories, where the data displayed above defines an equivalence inverse $\mathrm{h} g: \mathrm{h} B \rightarrow$ $\mathrm{h} A$ and natural isomorphisms encoded by the composite ${ }^{8}$ functors $$ \mathrm{h} A \xrightarrow{\mathrm{~h} \alpha} \mathrm{~h}\left(A^{\mathbb{I}}\right) \longrightarrow(\mathrm{h} A)^{\mathbb{I}} \quad \mathrm{h} B \xrightarrow{\mathrm{~h} \beta} \mathrm{~h}\left(B^{\mathbb{I}}\right) \longrightarrow(\mathrm{h} B)^{\mathbb{I}} $$
assumptions: $f: A \rightarrow B$ is an equivalence of quasi-categories
conclusions: the functor $\mathrm{h} f: \mathrm{h} A \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} B$ is an equivalence of categories

nodes.name: trivial fibration
nodes.statement: 1.1.25. Definition. A map $f: X \rightarrow Y$ between simplicial sets is a trivial fibration if it admits lifts against the boundary inclusions for all simplices\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-09_193_540_638_799} (1.1.26)\\ We write " ${ }^{2}$ »" to decorate trivial fibrations.
nodes.genus: A map $f: X \rightarrow Y$ between simplicial sets
differentia: it admits lifts against the boundary inclusions for all simplices

nodes.name: trivial fibrations lift against monomorphisms
nodes.statement: 1.1.27. Remark. The simplex boundary inclusions $\partial \Delta[n] \hookrightarrow \Delta[n]$ "cellularly generate" the monomorphisms of simplicial sets (see Definition C.2.4 and Lemma C.5.9). Hence the dual of Lemma C.2.3 implies that trivial fibrations lift against any monomorphism between simplicial sets. In particular, it follows that any trivial fibration $X \xrightarrow{\curvearrowright} Y$ is a split epimorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Boundary inclusions generate monomorphisms, so trivial fibrations lift against all monos and are split epimorphisms.

nodes.name: characterization of trivial fibrations of quasi-categories
nodes.statement: 1.1.28. Proposition. For a map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $f$ is a trivial fibration \item[(ii)] $f$ is both an isofibration and an equivalence \item[(iii)] $f$ is a split fiber homotopy equivalence: an isofibration admitting a section $s$ that is also an equivalence inverse via a homotopy $\alpha$ from $\mathrm{id}_{A}$ to $s f$ that composes with $f$ to the constant homotopy from $f$ to $f$.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-09_208_455_1575_839} \end{itemize}
also_stated_at: the trivial fibrations between quasi-categories are exactly those maps that are both isofibrations and equivalences.
assumptions: For a map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories
conclusions: the following are equivalent:
equivalent_conditions: $f$ is both an isofibration and an equivalence

$f$ is a split fiber homotopy equivalence: an isofibration admitting a section $s$ that is also an equivalence inverse via a homotopy $\alpha$ from $\mathrm{id}_{A}$ to $s f$ that composes with $f$ to the constant homotopy from $f$ to $f$.
nodes.statement_short: For quasi-categories: trivial fibration ⇔ isofibration and equivalence ⇔ split fiber homotopy equivalence.

nodes.name: closure properties of trivial fibrations
nodes.statement: As a class characterized by a right lifting property, the trivial fibrations are also closed under composition, product, pullback, limits of towers, and contain the isomorphisms.
conclusions: the trivial fibrations are also closed under composition, product, pullback, limits of towers, and contain the isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Leibniz exponential stability of trivial fibrations
nodes.statement: 1.1.29. Proposition. If $i: X \rightarrow Y$ is a monomorphism and $f: A \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration, then if either $f$ is a trivial fibration or if $i$ is in the class cellularly generated by the inner horn inclusions and the map $\mathbb{1} \leftrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ then the induced Leibniz exponential map $$ A^{Y} \xrightarrow{i \hbar f} B^{Y} \times_{B^{X}} A^{X} $$ a trivial fibration.
assumptions: $i$ is in the class cellularly generated by the inner horn inclusions and the map $\mathbb{1} \leftrightarrow \mathbb{I}$
conclusions: the induced Leibniz exponential map
the induced Leibniz exponential map

nodes.name: internal characterization of Kan complexes
nodes.statement: 1.1.30. Lemma. A quasi-category $A$ is a Kan complex if and only if the map $A^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow A^{2}$ induced by the inclusion $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ is a trivial fibration.
conclusions: is a Kan complex if and only if the map $A^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow A^{2}$ induced by the inclusion $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ is a trivial fibration.
equivalent_conditions: the map $A^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow A^{2}$ induced by the inclusion $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ is a trivial fibration.

nodes.name: A^I -> A^2 is an isofibration
nodes.statement: Note that Proposition 1.1.20 implies that $A^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow A^{2}$ is an isofibration.
conclusions: $A^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow A^{2}$ is an isofibration.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1.30
nodes.statement: Proof. The lifting property that characterizes trivial fibrations transposes to another lifting property, displayed below-right\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-10_219_1186_702_469}\\ that asserts that $A$ admits extensions along maps formed by taking the Leibniz product - also known as the pushout product - of a simplex boundary inclusion $\partial \Delta[n] \hookrightarrow \Delta[n]$ with the inclusion $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$. By Exercise 1.1.v(ii) the inclusion $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ is a sequential composite of pushouts of left outer horn inclusions. By Corollary D.3.11, a key step along the way to the proofs of Propositions 1.1.20 and 1.1.29, it follows that the Leibniz product is also a sequential composite of pushouts of left and inner horn inclusions. If $A$ is a Kan complex, then the extensions displayed above right exist, and, by transposing, the map $A^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow A^{2}$ is a trivial fibration. Conversely, if $A^{\mathbb{I}} \xrightarrow{{ }^{2}}$ is a trivial fibration then in particular it is surjective on vertices. Thus every arrow in $A$ is an isomorphism, and Corollary 1.1.15 tells us that $A$ must be a Kan complex.
nodes.statement_short: Transpose the lifting property to extensions along Leibniz products with $2\hookrightarrow\mathbb{I}$, built from outer horns; converse via Corollary 1.1.15.

nodes.name: Joyal model structure
nodes.statement: 1.1.31. Digression (the Joyal model structure). The category of simplicial sets bears a Quillen model structure, in the sense of Definition C.3.1, whose fibrant objects are exactly the quasi-categories and in which all objects are cofibrant. Between fibrant objects, the fibrations, weak equivalences, and trivial fibrations are precisely the isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations just introduced.
conclusions: The category of simplicial sets bears a Quillen model structure, in the sense of Definition C.3.1, whose fibrant objects are exactly the quasi-categories and in which all objects are cofibrant.

nodes.name: nerve functors from cosimplicial objects
nodes.statement: 1.1.i. Exercise ([103, §1.5]). Given any cosimplicial object $C: \boldsymbol{\Delta} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}$ valued in any category $\mathcal{E}$, there is an associated nerve functor $N_{C}$ defined by:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-10_149_360_2148_625}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-10_229_406_2144_1091} By construction $n$-simplices in $N_{C} E$ correspond to maps $C^{n} \rightarrow E$ in $\mathcal{E}$. Show that if $\mathcal{E}$ is cocomplete, then $N_{C}$ has a left adjoint defined as the left Kan extension of the functor $C$ along the Yoneda embedding よ: $\Delta \hookrightarrow$ sSet. This gives a second proof of Proposition 1.1.11.

nodes.name: homotopy relations on 1-simplices are equivalence relations
nodes.statement: 1.1.ii. Exercise (Boardman-Vogt [21]). Consider the set of 1-simplices in a quasi-category with initial vertex $a$ and final vertex $b$. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] Prove that the relation defined by $f \sim g$ if and only if there exists a 2 -simplex with boundary\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-11_157_233_586_385}\\ is an equivalence relation. \item[(ii)] Prove that the relation defined by $f \sim g$ if and only if there exists a 2-simplex with boundary\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-11_147_233_804_386}\\ is an equivalence relation. \item[(iii)] Prove that the equivalence relations defined by (i) and (ii) are the same. \end{itemize} This proves Lemma 1.1.9.

nodes.name: homotopy category of a quasi-category
nodes.statement: 1.1.iii. Exercise. Consider the free category on the reflexive directed graph $$ A_{1} \xrightarrow[\cdot \delta^{0}]{\xrightarrow{{ }^{+} \cdot \delta^{1}}-} A_{0}, $$ underlying a quasi-category $A$. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] Consider the binary relation that identifies sequences of composable 1-simplices with common source and common target whenever there exists a simplex of $A$ in which the sequences of 1-simplices define two paths from its initial vertex to its final vertex. Prove that this relation is stable under pre- and post-composition with 1-simplices and conclude that its transitive closure is a congruence: an equivalence relation that is closed under pre- and post-composition. ${ }^{9}$ \item[(ii)] Consider the congruence relation generated by imposing a composition relation $h=g \circ f$ witnessed by 2 -simplices\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-11_145_283_1727_919}\\ and prove that this coincides with the relation considered in (i). \item[(iii)] In the congruence relations of (i) and (ii), prove that every sequence of composable 1-simplices in $A$ is equivalent to a single 1-simplex. Conclude that every morphism in the quotient of the free category by this congruence relation is represented by a 1 -simplex in $A$. \item[(iv)] Prove that for any triple of 1-simplices $f, g, h$ in $A, h=g \circ f$ in the homotopy category $\mathrm{h} A$ of Definition 1.1.10 if and only if there exists a 2 -simplex with boundary\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-11_148_282_2198_920} \end{itemize} \footnotetext{${ }^{9}$ Given a congruence relation on the hom-sets of a 1-category, the quotient category can be formed by quotienting each hom-set (see [81, §II.8]). }This proves Lemma 1.1.12.

nodes.statement: 1.1.iv. Exercise. Show that any quasi-category in which inner horns admit unique fillers is isomorphic to the nerve of its homotopy category.

nodes.name: relative version of Corollary 1.1.16

Prove the relative version of Corollary 1.1.16: for any isofibration $p: A \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories and any $f: 2 \rightarrow A$ that defines an isomorphism in $A$ any homotopy coherent isomorphism in $B$ extending $p f$ lifts to a homotopy coherent isomorphism in $A$ extending $f$.

nodes.name: specializations of Proposition 1.1.20
nodes.statement: 1.1.vii. Exercise. Specialize Proposition 1.1.20 to prove the following: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] If $A$ is a quasi-category and $X$ is a simplicial set then $A^{X}$ is a quasi-category. \item[(ii)] If $A$ is a quasi-category and $X \hookrightarrow Y$ is a monomorphism then $A^{Y} \rightarrow A^{X}$ is an isofibration. \item[(iii)] If $A \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration and $X$ is a simplicial set then $A^{X} \rightarrow B^{X}$ is an isofibration. \end{itemize}
