nodes.name: trivial fibrations induce surjective equivalences
nodes.statement: 1.1.ix. Exercise. Prove that if $f: X \leadsto Y$ is a trivial fibration between quasi-categories then the functor $\mathrm{h} f: \mathrm{h} X \leadsto \mathrm{~h} Y$ is a surjective equivalence of categories.

nodes.name: ∞-cosmos
nodes.statement: 1.2.1. Definition $(\infty-\operatorname{cosmos})$. An $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is a category that is enriched over quasi-categories, ${ }^{13}$ meaning in particular that \begin{itemize} \item[-] its morphisms $f: A \rightarrow B$ define the vertices of a quasi-category denoted $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$ and referred to as a functor space, \end{itemize} that is also equipped with a specified collection of maps that we call isofibrations and denote by "→" satisfying the following two axioms: \begin{itemize} \item[] \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] (completeness) The quasi-categorically enriched category $\mathcal{K}$ possesses a terminal object, small products, pullbacks of isofibrations, limits of countable towers of isofibrations, and cotensors with simplicial sets, each of these limit notions satisfying a universal property that is enriched over simplicial sets. ${ }^{14}$ \item[(ii)] (isofibrations) The isofibrations contain all isomorphisms and any map whose codomain is the terminal object; are closed under composition, product, pullback, forming inverse limits of towers, and Leibniz cotensors with monomorphisms of simplicial sets; and have the property that if $f: A \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration and $X$ is any object then $\operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ is an isofibration of quasi-categories. \end{itemize} \end{itemize}
nodes.genus: category that is enriched over quasi-categories
differentia: (completeness) The quasi-categorically enriched category $\mathcal{K}$ possesses a terminal object, small products, pullbacks of isofibrations, limits of countable towers of isofibrations, and cotensors with simplicial sets, each of these limit notions satisfying a universal property that is enriched over simplicial sets.
(isofibrations) The isofibrations contain all isomorphisms and any map whose codomain is the terminal object;
nodes.statement_short: An ∞-cosmos: a quasi-categorically enriched category with isofibrations, closed under cosmological limits (terminal object, products, pullbacks, towers, cotensors).

nodes.name: cosmological limit notions
nodes.statement: For ease of reference, we refer to the simplicially enriched limits of diagrams of isofibrations enumerated in (i) as the cosmological limit notions.

nodes.name: equivalences and trivial fibrations in an ∞-cosmos
nodes.statement: 1.2.2. Definition. In an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$, a morphism $f: A \rightarrow B$ is \begin{itemize} \item[-] an equivalence just when the induced map $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\sim \operatorname{Fun}(X, B) \text { on functor spaces is an }}$ equivalence of quasi-categories for all $X \in \mathcal{K}$, and \item[-] a trivial fibration just when $f$ is both an isofibration and an equivalence. \end{itemize} These classes are denoted by "→" and "→»", respectively.
nodes.statement_short: In an ∞-cosmos, $f$ is an equivalence if $\mathrm{Fun}(X,f)$ is an equivalence of quasi-categories for all $X$; trivial fibration = isofibration + equivalence.

nodes.name: ∞-category (technical term)
nodes.statement: 1.2.3. Convention ( $\infty$-category, as a technical term). Henceforth, we recast $\infty$-category as a technical term to refer to an object in an arbitrary ambient $\infty$-cosmos.
also_stated_at: To focus this abstract theory on its intended interpretation, we recast " $\infty$-category" as a technical term, reserved to mean an object of some $\infty$-cosmos.

nodes.name: ∞-functor
nodes.statement: Similarly, we use the term $\infty$-functor - or more commonly the elision "functor" - to refer to a morphism $f: A \rightarrow B$ in an $\infty$-cosmos.

nodes.name: simplicial category
nodes.statement: 1.2.4. Digression (simplicial categories, § A.2). A simplicial category $\mathcal{A}$ is given by categories $\mathcal{A}_{n}$, with a common set of objects and whose arrows are called $n$-arrows, that assemble into a diagram $\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\mathrm{op}} \rightarrow$ Cat of identity-on-objects functors \begin{equation*} \cdots \mathcal{A}_{3} \underset{-\cdot \delta^{1}}{\stackrel{-\cdot \delta^{3}}{\rightleftarrows} \cdot \delta^{2} \longrightarrow} \mathcal{A}_{2} \underset{-\cdot \delta^{1}}{\stackrel{-\delta^{2}}{\leftrightarrows} \cdot \delta^{1} \longrightarrow} \mathcal{A}_{1} \underset{-\cdot \delta^{0}}{\stackrel{-\cdot \delta^{1}}{\leftrightarrows}} \underset{\rightarrow}{\stackrel{\leftarrow \cdot \delta^{0}}{\longrightarrow}} \mathcal{A}_{0}=: \mathcal{A} \tag{1.2.5} \end{equation*} The category $\mathcal{A}_{0}$ of 0-arrows is the underlying category of the simplicial category $\mathcal{A}$, which forgets the higher dimensional simplicial structure. The data of a simplicial category can equivalently be encoded by a simplicially enriched category with a set of objects and a simplicial set $\mathcal{A}(x, y)$ of morphisms between each ordered pair of objects: an $n$-arrow in $\mathcal{A}_{n}$ from $x$ to $y$ corresponds to an $n$-simplex in $\mathcal{A}(x, y)$ (see Exercise 1.2.i). Each endo-hom space contains a distinguished identity 0-arrow (the degenerate images of which define the corresponding identity $n$-arrows) and composition is required to define a simplicial map $$ \mathcal{A}(y, z) \times \mathcal{A}(x, y) \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}(x, z) $$ the single map encoding the compositions in each of the categories $\mathcal{A}_{n}$ and also the functoriality of the diagram (1.2.5). The composition is required to be associative and unital, in a sense expressed by the commutative diagrams of simplicial sets $$ \begin{gathered} \mathcal{A}(y, z) \times \mathcal{A}(x, y) \times \mathcal{A}(w, x) \xrightarrow{\circ \times \mathrm{id}} \mathcal{A}(x, z) \times \mathcal{A}(w, x) \\ \downarrow \\ \begin{array}{l} \mathrm{id} \times \circ \downarrow \\ \mathcal{A}(y, z) \times \mathcal{A}(w, y) \longrightarrow \end{array} \end{gathered} $$ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-14_225_732_1393_1144}\\ On account of the equivalence between these two presentations, the terms "simplicial category" and "simplicially enriched category" are generally taken to be synonyms.
nodes.statement_short: A simplicial category: categories $\mathcal{A}_n$ of $n$-arrows on common objects forming a simplicial diagram; equivalently a simplicially enriched category.

nodes.name: simplicial category as a simplicial diagram of categories
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \cdots \mathcal{A}_{3} \underset{-\cdot \delta^{1}}{\stackrel{-\cdot \delta^{3}}{\rightleftarrows} \cdot \delta^{2} \longrightarrow} \mathcal{A}_{2} \underset{-\cdot \delta^{1}}{\stackrel{-\delta^{2}}{\leftrightarrows} \cdot \delta^{1} \longrightarrow} \mathcal{A}_{1} \underset{-\cdot \delta^{0}}{\stackrel{-\cdot \delta^{1}}{\leftrightarrows}} \underset{\rightarrow}{\stackrel{\leftarrow \cdot \delta^{0}}{\longrightarrow}} \mathcal{A}_{0}=: \mathcal{A} \tag{1.2.5} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: underlying category of an ∞-cosmos
nodes.statement: In particular, the underlying category $\mathcal{K}_{0}$ of an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is the category whose objects are the $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ and whose morphisms are the 0-arrows, i.e., the vertices in the functor spaces.

nodes.name: simplicial cotensor
nodes.statement: 1.2.6. Digression (simplicially enriched limits, §A.4-A.5). Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a simplicial category. The cotensor of an object $A \in \mathcal{A}$ by a simplicial set $U$ is characterized by a natural isomorphism of simplicial sets \begin{equation*} \mathcal{A}\left(X, A^{U}\right) \cong \mathcal{A}(X, A)^{U} \tag{1.2.7} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: universal property of the simplicial cotensor
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \mathcal{A}\left(X, A^{U}\right) \cong \mathcal{A}(X, A)^{U} \tag{1.2.7} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: simplicially enriched limit
nodes.statement: The other simplicial limit notions postulated by axiom 1.2.1(i) are conical, which is the term used for ordinary 1-categorical limit shapes that satisfy an enriched analog of the usual universal property (see Definition A.5.2). Such limits also define limits in the underlying category, but the usual universal property is strengthened. By applying the covariant representable functor $\mathcal{A}(X,-): \mathcal{A}_{0} \rightarrow s \mathcal{S} e t$ to a limit cone $\left(\lim _{j \in J} A_{j} \rightarrow A_{j}\right)_{j \in J}$ in $\mathcal{A}_{0}$, we obtain a natural comparison map \begin{equation*} \mathcal{A}\left(X, \lim _{j \in J} A_{j}\right) \longrightarrow \lim _{j \in J} \mathcal{A}\left(X, A_{j}\right) . \tag{1.2.8} \end{equation*} We say that $\lim _{j \in J} A_{j}$ defines a simplicially enriched limit if and only if (1.2.8) is an isomorphism of simplicial sets for all $X \in \mathcal{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: A conical limit is simplicially enriched if the comparison map (1.2.8) on hom spaces is an isomorphism of simplicial sets.

nodes.name: comparison map for conical limits
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \mathcal{A}\left(X, \lim _{j \in J} A_{j}\right) \longrightarrow \lim _{j \in J} \mathcal{A}\left(X, A_{j}\right) . \tag{1.2.8} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: flexible weighted limits in ∞-cosmoi
nodes.statement: 1.2.9. Preview (flexible weighted limits in $\infty$-cosmoi). The axiom 1.2.1(i) implies that any $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ admits all flexible limits, a much larger class of simplicially enriched "weighted" limits (see Definition 6.2.1 and Proposition 6.2.8).
conclusions: any $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ admits all flexible limits

nodes.name: the ∞-cosmos of quasi-categories
nodes.statement: 1.2.10. Proposition (the $\infty$-cosmos of quasi-categories). The full subcategory QCat $\subset$ sSet of quasi-cat-egories defines an $\infty$-cosmos in which the isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations coincide with the classes already bearing these names.
conclusions: The full subcategory QCat $\subset$ sSet of quasi-cat-egories defines an $\infty$-cosmos in which the isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations coincide with the classes already bearing these names.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.2.10
nodes.statement: Proof. The subcategory QCat $\subset$ sSet inherits its simplicial enrichment from the cartesian closed category of simplicial sets: by Proposition 1.1.20, whenever $A$ and $B$ are quasi-categories, $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B):=B^{A}$ is again a quasi-category. The cosmological limits postulated in 1.2.1(i) exist in the ambient category of simplicial sets. ${ }^{16}$ For instance, the defining universal property of the simplicial cotensor (1.2.7) is satisfied by the exponentials of simplicial sets. Moreover, since the category of simplicial sets is cartesian closed, each of the conical limits is simplicially enriched in the sense discussed in Digression 1.2.6 (see Exercise 1.2.ii and Proposition A.5.4). We now argue that the full subcategory of quasi-categories inherits all these limit notions and at the same time establish the stability of the isofibrations under the formation of these limits. In fact, this latter property helps to prove the former. To see this, note that a simplicial set is a quasi-category if and only if the map from it to the point is an isofibration. More generally, if the codomain of any isofibration is a quasi-category then its domain must be as well. So if any of the maps in a limit cone over a diagram of quasi-categories are isofibrations, then it follows that the limit is itself a quasi-category. Since the isofibrations are characterized by a right lifting property, Lemma C.2.3 implies that the isofibrations contains all isomorphism and are closed under composition, product, pullback, and forming inverse limits of towers. In particular, the full subcategory of quasi-categories possesses these \footnotetext{${ }^{16}$ Any category of presheaves is cartesian closed, complete, and cocomplete - a "cosmos" in the sense of Bénabou. } limits. This verifies all of the axioms of 1.2.1(i) and 1.2.1(ii) except for the last two: Leibniz closure and closure under exponentiation $(-)^{X}$. These last closure properties are established in Proposition 1.1.20, and in fact by Exercise 1.1.vii, the former subsumes the latter . This completes the verification of the $\infty$-cosmos axioms. It remains to check that the equivalences and trivial fibrations coincide with those maps defined by 1.1.23 and 1.1.25. By Proposition 1.1.28 the latter coincidence follows from the former, so it remains only to show that the equivalences of 1.1.23 coincide with the representably defined equivalences: those maps of quasi-categories $f: A \rightarrow B$ for which $A^{X} \rightarrow B^{X}$ is an equivalence of quasi-categories in the sense of Definition 1.1.23. Taking $X=\Delta[0]$, we see immediately that representably defined equivalences are equivalences, and the converse holds since the exponential $(-)^{X}$ preserves the data defining a simplicial homotopy.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the axioms: enrichment by Prop. 1.1.20, limits from sSet with isofibration stability via right lifting; equivalences match by Prop. 1.1.28.

nodes.name: the ∞-cosmos of categories
nodes.statement: 1.2.11. Proposition (the $\infty$-cosmos of categories). The category Cat of 1 -categories defines an $\infty$-cosmos whose isofibrations are the isofibrations: functors satisfying the displayed right lifting property:} \includegraphics[alt={},max width=\textwidth]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-16_172_207_1156_962} \end{center} \end{figure} The equivalences are the equivalences of categories and the trivial fibrations are surjective equivalences: equivalences of categories that are also surjective on objects.
conclusions: The category Cat of 1 -categories defines an $\infty$-cosmos whose isofibrations are the isofibrations: functors satisfying the displayed right lifting property:
The equivalences are the equivalences of categories and the trivial fibrations are surjective equivalences: equivalences of categories that are also surjective on objects.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.2.11
nodes.statement: Proof. It is well-known that the 2-category of categories is complete (and in fact also cocomplete) as a Cat-enriched category (see Definition A.6.17 or [67]). The categorically enriched category of categories becomes a quasi-categorically enriched category by applying the nerve functor to the homcategories (see §A.7). Since the nerve functor is a right adjoint, it follows formally that these 2-categorical limits become simplicially enriched limits. In particular, as proscribed in Proposition A.7.8, the cotensor of a category $A$ by a simplicial set $U$ is defined to be the functor category $A^{\text {hU }}$. This completes the verification of axiom (i). Since the class of isofibrations is characterized by a right lifting property, Lemma C.2.3 implies that the isofibrations are closed under all of the limit constructions of 1.2.1(ii) except for the last two, and by Exercise 1.1.vii, the Leibniz closure subsumes the closure under exponentiation. To verify that isofibrations of categories $f: A \rightarrow B$ are stable under forming Leibniz cotensors with monomorphisms of simplicial sets $i: U \hookrightarrow V$, we must solve the lifting problem below-left\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-16_234_975_2081_575}\\ which transposes to the lifting problem above-right, which we can solve by hand. Here the map $\beta$ defines a natural isomorphism between $f s: \mathrm{h} V \rightarrow B$ and a second functor. Our task is to lift this\\ to a natural isomorphism $\gamma$ from $s$ to another functor that extends the natural isomorphism $\alpha$ along $\mathrm{h} i: \mathrm{h} U \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} V$. Note this functor hi need not be an inclusion, but it is injective on objects, which is enough. We define the components of $\gamma$ by cases. If an object $v \in \mathrm{~h} V$ is equal to $i(u)$ for some $u \in \mathrm{~h} U$ define $\gamma_{i(u)}:=\alpha_{u}$; otherwise, use the fact that $f$ is an isofibration to define $\gamma_{v}$ to be any lift of the isomorphism $\beta_{v}$ to an isomorphism in $A$ with domain $s(v)$. The data of the map $\gamma: \mathrm{h} V \times \mathbb{I} \rightarrow A$ also entails the specification of the functor $\mathrm{h} V \rightarrow A$ that is the codomain of the natural isomorphism $\gamma$. On objects, this functor is given by $v \mapsto \operatorname{cod}\left(\gamma_{v}\right)$. On morphisms, this functor defined in the unique way that makes $\gamma$ into a natural transformation: $$ \left(k: v \rightarrow v^{\prime}\right) \mapsto \gamma_{v^{\prime}} \circ s(k) \circ \gamma_{v}^{-1} . $$ This completes the proof that $C a t$ defines an $\infty$-cosmos. Since the nerve of a functor category, such as $A^{\mathbb{I}}$, is isomorphic to the exponential between their nerves, the equivalences of categories coincide with the equivalences of Definition 1.1.23. It follows that the equivalences in the $\infty$-cosmos of categories coincide with equivalences of categories, and since the surjective equivalences are the intersection of the equivalences and the isofibrations, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: 2-categorical limits in Cat become simplicial limits under the nerve; Leibniz stability of isofibrations by lifting a natural isomorphism by hand.

nodes.name: the ∞-cosmos of Kan complexes
nodes.statement: 1.2.12. Proposition (the $\infty$-cosmos of Kan complexes). The category Kan of Kan complexes defines an $\infty$-cosmos whose isofibrations are the Kan fibrations: maps that lift against all horn inclusions $\Lambda^{k}[n] \hookrightarrow \Delta[n]$ for $n \geq 1$ and $0 \leq k \leq n$.
conclusions: The category Kan of Kan complexes defines an $\infty$-cosmos whose isofibrations are the Kan fibrations:

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.2.12
nodes.statement: Proof. By Proposition 1.1.18, an isofibration between Kan complexes is a Kan fibration. Conversely, since the homotopy coherent isomorphism $\mathbb{I}$ can be built from the point $\mathbb{1}$ by attaching fillers to a sequence of outer horns, all Kan fibrations define isofibrations. This shows that between Kan complexes, isofibrations and Kan fibrations coincide. So to show that the category of Kan complexes inherits an $\infty$-cosmos structure by restriction from the $\infty$-cosmos of quasi-categories, we need only verify that the full subcategory Kan ↪ QCat is closed under all of the limit constructions of axiom 1.2.1(i). For the conical limits, the argument mirrors the one given in the proof of Proposition 1.2.10, while the closure under cotensors is a consequence of Corollary D.3.11, which implies that the Kan complexes also define an exponential ideal in the category of simplicial sets. The remaining axiom 1.2.1(ii) is inherited from the analogous properties established for quasi-categories in Proposition 1.2.10.
nodes.statement_short: Isofibrations and Kan fibrations coincide between Kan complexes; then restrict the ∞-cosmos structure of QCat, checking closure under limits.

nodes.name: a source of ∞-cosmoi in nature
nodes.statement: 1.2.13. Digression (a source of $\infty$-cosmoi in nature). As explained in §E.1, certain easily described properties of a model category imply that the full subcategory of fibrant objects defines an $\infty$-cosmos whose isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations are the fibrations, weak equivalences, and trivial fibrations between fibrant objects. Namely, any model category that is enriched as such over the Joyal model structure on simplicial sets in which all fibrant objects are cofibrant presents an $\infty$-cosmos (see Proposition E.1.1). This model-categorical enrichment over quasi-categories can be defined when the model category is cartesian closed and equipped with a right Quillen adjoint to the Joyal model structure on simplicial sets whose left adjoint preserves finite products (see Corollary E.1.4). In this case, the right adjoint becomes the underlying quasi-category functor (see Proposition 1.3.4(ii)) and\\ the $\infty$-cosmoi so-produced is cartesian closed (see Definition 1.2.23). The $\infty$-cosmoi listed in Example 1.2.24 all arise in this way.
nodes.statement_short: Model categories enriched over the Joyal model structure with fibrant objects cofibrant present ∞-cosmoi (Appendix E).

nodes.name: stability of trivial fibrations
nodes.statement: 1.2.14. Lemma (stability of trivial fibrations). The trivial fibrations in an $\infty$-cosmos define a subcategory containing the isomorphisms and are stable under product, pullback, and forming inverse limits of towers. Moreover, the Leibniz cotensors of any trivial fibration with a monomorphism of simplicial sets is a trivial fibration as is the Leibniz cotensor of an isofibration with a map in the class cellularly generated by the inner horn inclusions and the map $\mathbb{1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$, and if $E \leadsto B$ is a trivial fibration then so is $\operatorname{Fun}(X, E) \leadsto \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$.
conclusions: The trivial fibrations in an $\infty$-cosmos define a subcategory containing the isomorphisms and are stable under product, pullback, and forming inverse limits of towers.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial fibrations in an ∞-cosmos are closed under composition, products, pullback, towers, Leibniz cotensors and $\mathrm{Fun}(X,-)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.2.14
nodes.statement: Proof. We prove these statements in the reverse order. By axiom 1.2.1(ii) and the definition of the trivial fibrations in an $\infty$-cosmos, we know that if $E \xrightarrow{ } B$ is a trivial fibration then $\operatorname{Fun}(X, E) \xrightarrow{\leadsto}$ $\operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ is both an isofibration and an equivalence, and hence by Proposition 1.1.28 a trivial fibration. For stability under the remaining constructions, we know in each case that the maps in question are isofibrations in the $\infty$-cosmos; it remains to show only that the maps are also equivalences. The equivalences in an $\infty$-cosmos are defined to be the maps that $\operatorname{Fun}(X,-)$ carries to equivalences of quasi-categories, so it suffices to verify that trivial fibrations of quasi-categories satisfy the corresponding stability properties. For the Leibniz stability properties, this is established in Proposition 1.1.29, while the remaining properties are covered by Lemma C.2.3.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via representable functors to trivial fibrations of quasi-categories, then apply Propositions 1.1.28, 1.1.29 and Lemma C.2.3.

nodes.name: equivalences are homotopy equivalences
nodes.statement: 1.2.15. Lemma (equivalences are homotopy equivalences). A map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between $\infty$-categories in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is an equivalence if and only if it extends to the data of a "homotopy equivalence" with the free-living isomorphism II serving as the interval: that is, if there exist maps $g: B \rightarrow A$\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-18_317_767_1550_682} (1.2.16)\\ in the $\infty$-cosmos.
assumptions: A map $f: A \rightarrow B$ between $\infty$-categories in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$
conclusions: is an equivalence if and only if it extends to the data of a "homotopy equivalence" with the free-living isomorphism II serving as the interval:
equivalent_conditions: it extends to the data of a "homotopy equivalence" with the free-living isomorphism II serving as the interval:

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.2.15
nodes.statement: Proof. By hypothesis, if $f: A \rightarrow B$ defines an equivalence in the $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ then the induced map on post-composition $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(B, A) \xrightarrow{\sim \operatorname{Fun}(B, B) \text { is an equivalence of quasi-categories in the sense }}$ of Definition 1.1.23. Evaluating the inverse equivalence $\widetilde{g}: \operatorname{Fun}(B, B) \xrightarrow{\Rightarrow} \operatorname{Fun}(B, A)$ and homotopy $\widetilde{\beta}: \operatorname{Fun}(B, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)^{\mathbb{I}}$ at the 0-arrow $\operatorname{id}_{B} \in \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$, we obtain a 0-arrow $g: B \rightarrow A$ together with an isomorphism $\beta: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$ from the composite $f g$ to $\operatorname{id}_{B}$. By the defining universal property of the cotensor (1.2.7), this isomorphism internalizes to define the map $\beta: B \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ in $\mathcal{K}$ displayed on the right of (1.2.16). Now the hypothesis that $f$ is an equivalence also provides an equivalence of quasi-categories $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$, and the map $\beta f: A \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ represents an isomorphism in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$ from $f g f$ to $f$. Since $f_{*}$ is an equivalence, we conclude from Remark 1.1.24 that $\mathrm{id}_{A}$ and $g f$ are isomorphic in\\ the quasi-category $\operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ : explicitly, such an isomorphism may be defined by applying the inverse equivalence $\tilde{h}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ and composing with the components at $\operatorname{id}_{A}, g f \in \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ of the isomorphism $\widetilde{\alpha}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, A) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)^{\mathbb{I}}$ from $\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Fun}(A, A)}$ to $\widetilde{h} f_{*}$. Now by Corollary 1.1.16 this isomorphism is represented by a map $\mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ from $\operatorname{id}_{A}$ to $g f$, which internalizes to a map $\alpha: A \rightarrow A^{\mathbb{I}}$ in $\mathcal{K}$ displayed on the left of (1.2.16). The converse is easy: the simplicial cotensor construction commutes with $\operatorname{Fun}(X,-)$, so a homotopy equivalence (1.2.16) induces a homotopy equivalence of quasi-categories as in Definition 1.1.23.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate inverse equivalences of $f_*$ on functor spaces at identities to get $g$, $\beta$, then $\alpha$ via Remark 1.1.24 and Corollary 1.1.16.

nodes.name: retracts and 2-of-3 for equivalences
nodes.statement: 1.2.17. Lemma. The equivalences in an $\infty$-cosmos are closed under retracts and satisfy the 2 -of-3 property: given a composable pair of functors and their composite, if any two of these are equivalences so is the third.
conclusions: The equivalences in an $\infty$-cosmos are closed under retracts and satisfy the 2 -of-3 property:

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 1.2.17 via quasi-categories
nodes.statement: By the representable definition of equivalences and functoriality, Lemma 1.2.17 follows easily from the corresponding results for equivalences between quasi-categories (see Exercise 1.1.viii).
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: reduce representably to the quasi-categorical case (Exercise 1.1.viii).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.2.17
nodes.statement: Proof. Let $f: A \xrightarrow{口} B$ be an equivalence equipped with the data of (1.2.16) and consider a retract diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-19_267_389_1046_867}\\ By Lemma 1.2.15, to prove that $h: C \rightarrow D$ is an equivalence, it suffices to construct the data of an inverse homotopy equivalence. To that end define $k: D \rightarrow C$ to be the composite $v g s$ and then observe from the commutative diagrams\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-19_526_600_1496_427}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-19_518_584_1498_1107}\\ that $v^{\mathbb{I}} \alpha u: C \rightarrow C^{\mathbb{I}}$ and $t^{\mathbb{I}} \beta s: D \rightarrow D^{\mathbb{I}}$ define the required homotopy coherent isomorphisms.\\ Via Lemma 1.2.15, the 2-of-3 property for equivalences follows from the fact that the set of isomorphisms in a quasi-category is closed under composition. Homotopy coherent isomorphisms in a quasi-category represent isomorphisms in the homotopy category, whose composite in the homotopy category is then an isomorphism, which can be lifted to a representing homotopy coherent isomorphism by Corollary 1.1.16. ${ }^{17}$ We now apply this to the homotopy coherent isomorphisms in the functor spaces of an $\infty$-cosmos that form part of the data of an equivalence of $\infty$-categories. \footnotetext{${ }^{17}$ In fact, by Example D.5.5, homotopy coherent isomorphisms can be composed directly, but we do not need this here. }To prove that equivalences are closed under composition, consider a composable pair of equivalences with their inverse equivalences $$ A \underset{\stackrel{\sim}{k}}{\stackrel{f}{\rightleftarrows}} B \underset{\stackrel{\sim}{h}}{\stackrel{g}{\underset{\sim}{\sim}}} C $$ The equivalence data of Lemma 1.2.15 defines isomorphisms $\alpha: \operatorname{id}_{A} \cong k f \in \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ and $\gamma: \operatorname{id}_{B} \cong$ $h g \in \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$, the latter of which whiskers to define $k \gamma f: k f \cong k h g f \in \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$. Composing these, we obtain an isomorphism $\operatorname{id}_{A} \cong \operatorname{khg} f \in \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$, witnessing that $k h$ defines a left equivalence inverse of $g f$. The other isomorphism is constructed similarly. To prove that the equivalences are closed under right cancelation, consider a diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_203_358_747_882}\\ with $k$ an inverse equivalence to $f$ and $\ell$ and inverse equivalence to $g f$. We claim that $f \ell$ defines an inverse equivalence to $g$. One of the required isomorphisms $\mathrm{id}_{C} \cong g f \ell$ is given already. The other is obtained by composing three isomorphisms in $\operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$ $$ \operatorname{id}_{B} \xrightarrow[\bar{z}]{\beta^{-1}} f k \xrightarrow[\bar{z}]{f \delta k} f \ell g f k \xrightarrow[\bar{z}]{f \ell g \beta} f \ell g . $$ The proof of stability of equivalence under left cancelation is dual.
nodes.statement_short: Using Lemma 1.2.15, build homotopy-equivalence data for retracts, composites and cancellations by composing homotopy coherent isomorphisms.

nodes.name: trivial fibrations split
nodes.statement: 1.2.18. Lemma (trivial fibrations split). Every trivial fibration admits a section\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_173_203_1443_964}\\ that defines a split fiber homotopy equivalence\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_265_449_1707_832}\\ and conversely any isofibration that defines a split fiber homotopy equivalence is a trivial fibration.
conclusions: Every trivial fibration admits a section
any isofibration that defines a split fiber homotopy equivalence is a trivial fibration.
Every trivial fibration admits a section
any isofibration that defines a split fiber homotopy equivalence is a trivial fibration.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.2.18
nodes.statement: Proof. If $p: E \leadsto B$ is a trivial fibration, then by the final stability property of Lemma 1.2.14, so is $p_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, E) \xrightarrow{\Rightarrow} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ for any $\infty$-category $X$. By Definition 1.1.25, we may solve the lifting problem below-left\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_229_483_2221_483}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_225_552_2218_1088}\\ to find a map $s: B \rightarrow E$ so that $p s=\mathrm{id}_{B}$, and then solve the lifting problem above-right to construct the desired fibered homotopy. The converse is immediate from Lemma 1.2.15.
nodes.statement_short: Solve lifting problems against $\mathrm{Fun}(X,p)$ to get a section and fibered homotopy; converse by Lemma 1.2.15.

nodes.name: Brown factorization lemma
nodes.statement: 1.2.19. Lemma (Brown factorization lemma). Any functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ in an $\infty$-cosmos may be factored as an equivalence followed by an isofibration, where this equivalence is constructed as a section of a trivial fibration.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-21_214_378_597_872} (1.2.20)\\ Moreover, $f$ is an equivalence if and only if the isofibration $p$ is a trivial fibration.
assumptions: Any functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ in an $\infty$-cosmos
conclusions: may be factored as an equivalence followed by an isofibration, where this equivalence is constructed as a section of a trivial fibration.
$f$ is an equivalence if and only if the isofibration $p$ is a trivial fibration.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.2.19
nodes.statement: Proof. The displayed factorization is constructed by the pullback of an isofibration formed by the simplicial cotensor of the inclusion $\mathbb{1}+\mathbb{1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ into the $\infty$-category $B$.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-21_359_570_1018_780}\\ Note the map $q$ is a pullback of the trivial fibration $\mathrm{ev}_{0}: B^{\mathbb{I}} \xrightarrow{\text { ⇒ }} B$ and is hence a trivial fibration. Its section $s$, constructed by applying the universal property of the pullback to the displayed cone with summit $A$, is thus an equivalence by the 2-of-3 property. Again by 2-of-3, it follows that $f$ is an equivalence if and only if $p$ is.
nodes.statement_short: Factor through the pullback of $B^{\mathbb{I}}\to B\times B$; the section of a trivial fibration is an equivalence by 2-of-3.

nodes.name: equivalences satisfy the 2-of-6 property
nodes.statement: 1.2.21. Remark (equivalences satisfy the 2-of-6 property). In fact the equivalences in any $\infty$-cosmos satisfy the stronger 2-of-6 property: for any composable triple of functors\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-21_306_364_1744_878}\\ if $g f$ and $h g$ are equivalences then $f, g, h$, and $h g f$ are too. An argument of Blumberg and Mandell [20, 6.4] reproduced in Proposition C.1.8 uses Lemmas 1.2.17, 1.2.18, and 1.2.19 to prove that the equivalences have the 2-of-6 property (see Corollary C.1.9).
nodes.statement_short: Equivalences in an ∞-cosmos satisfy 2-of-6, by an argument of Blumberg–Mandell using Lemmas 1.2.17–1.2.19.

nodes.name: sliced ∞-cosmoi
nodes.statement: 1.2.22. Proposition (sliced $\infty$-cosmoi). For any $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ and any $\infty$-category $B \in \mathcal{K}$ there is an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ of isofibrations over $B$ whose \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] objects are isofibrations $p: E \rightarrow B$ with codomain $B$ \item[(ii)] functor spaces, say from $p: E \rightarrow B$ to $q: F \rightarrow B$, are defined by pullback\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-22_195_707_596_707}\\ and abbreviated to $\operatorname{Fun}_{B}(E, F)$ when the specified isofibrations are clear from context \item[(iii)] isofibrations are commutative triangles of isofibrations over $B$\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-22_140_248_934_937} \item[(iv)] terminal object is id: $B \rightarrow B$ and products are defined by the pullback along the diagonal\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-22_216_346_1173_892} \item[(v)] pullbacks and limits of towers of isofibrations are created by the forgetful functor $\mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$ \item[(vi)] simplicial cotensor of $p: E \rightarrow B$ with $U \in$ sSet is constructed by the pullback\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-22_199_335_1535_899} \item[(vii)] and in which a map over $B$\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-22_156_248_1808_938}\\ is an equivalence in the $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ if and only if $f$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: there is an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ of isofibrations over $B$ whose
nodes.statement_short: The isofibrations over a fixed $B$ form an ∞-cosmos $\mathcal{K}_{/B}$, with limits created by pullback and equivalences detected in $\mathcal{K}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.2.22
nodes.statement: Proof. The functor spaces are quasi-categories since axiom 1.2.1(ii) asserts that for any isofibration $q: F \rightarrow B$ in $\mathcal{K}$ the map $q_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(E, F) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(E, B)$ is an isofibration of quasi-categories. Other parts of this axiom imply that each of the limit constructions - such as the products and cotensors constructed in (iv) and (vi) - define isofibrations over $B$. The closure properties of the isofibrations in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ follow from the corresponding ones in $\mathcal{K}$. The most complicated of these is the Leibniz cotensor stability of the isofibrations in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$, which follows from the corresponding property in $\mathcal{K}$, since for a monomorphism of simplicial sets $i: X \hookrightarrow Y$ and an isofibration $r$ over $B$ as in (iii) above, the map $i \widehat{\Pi_{B}} r$ is constructed by pulling back $i \widehat{\pitchfork} r$ along $\Delta: B \rightarrow B^{Y}$. The fact that the above constructions define simplicially enriched limits in a simplicially enriched slice category are standard from enriched category theory. It remains only to verify that the equivalences in the $\infty$-cosmos of isofibrations are created by the forgetful functor $\mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$. Suppose first that the map $f$ displayed in (vii) defines an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$. Then for any isofibration $s: A \rightarrow B$ the induced map on functor spaces in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ is defined by the pullback:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-23_268_952_517_585}\\ Since $f$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$, the map $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, E) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, F)$ is an equivalence, and so it follows that the induced map on fibers over $s$ is an equivalence as well. ${ }^{18}$ For the converse implication, we appeal to Lemma 1.2.15. If $f: E \rightarrow F$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ then it admits a homotopy inverse in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$. The inverse equivalence $g: F \rightarrow E$ also defines an inverse equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$ and the required simplicial homotopies in $\mathcal{K}$ $$ E \xrightarrow{\alpha} \mathbb{I} \pitchfork_{B} p \longrightarrow E^{\mathbb{I}} \quad F \xrightarrow{\beta} \mathbb{I} \pitchfork_{B} q \rightarrow F^{\mathbb{I}} $$ are defined by composing with the top horizontal leg of the pullback defining the cotensor in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$.
nodes.statement_short: Axioms from those of $\mathcal{K}$ by pullback; equivalences created by the forgetful functor, converse via Lemma 1.2.15.

nodes.name: cartesian closed ∞-cosmos
nodes.statement: 1.2.23. Definition (cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmoi). An $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is cartesian closed if the product bifunctor $-\times-: \mathcal{K} \times \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$ extends to a simplicially enriched two-variable adjunction $$ \operatorname{Fun}(A \times B, C) \cong \operatorname{Fun}\left(A, C^{B}\right) \cong \operatorname{Fun}\left(B, C^{A}\right) $$ in which the right adjoints $(-)^{A}: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$ preserve isofibrations for all $A \in \mathcal{K}$.
differentia: the product bifunctor $-\times-: \mathcal{K} \times \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$ extends to a simplicially enriched two-variable adjunction

nodes.name: quasi-categories form a cartesian closed ∞-cosmos
nodes.statement: For instance, the $\infty$-cosmos of quasi-categories is cartesian closed, with the exponentials defined as (special cases of) simplicial cotensors.

nodes.name: ∞-cosmoi of (∞,1)-categories
nodes.statement: 1.2.24. Example ( $\infty$-cosmoi of $(\infty, 1)$-categories; §E.2). The following models of $(\infty, 1)$-categories define cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmoi: \footnotetext{${ }^{18}$ The stability of equivalences between isofibrations under pullback can be proven either as a consequence of Lemmas 1.2.14 and 1.2.19 using standard techniques from simplicial homotopy theory (see Lemma C.1.11) or by arguing 2-categorically (see Proposition 3.3.4).\\ ${ }^{19}$ Other advantages of this convenient notational conflation are discussed in §2.3 and in Proposition 10.3.5. } \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] Rezk's complete Segal spaces define the objects of an $\infty-\cos \operatorname{mos} \mathcal{C S S}$, in which the isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations are the corresponding classes of the model structure of [100]. ${ }^{20}$ \item[(ii)] The Segal categories defined by Dwyer, Kan, and Smith [38] and developed by Hirschowitz and Simpson [56] define the objects of an $\infty$-cosmos Segal, in which the isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations are the corresponding classes of the model structure of [13, 90]. ${ }^{21}$ \item[(iii)] The 1-complicial sets of [129], equivalently the "naturally marked quasi-categories" of [78], define the objects of an $\infty$-cosmos 1-Comp in which the isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations are the corresponding classes of the model structure from either of these sources. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Complete Segal spaces, Segal categories and 1-complicial sets form cartesian closed ∞-cosmoi.

nodes.name: opposite simplicial set
nodes.statement: 1.2.25. Definition (co-dual $\infty$-cosmoi). There is an identity-on-objects involutive functor $(-)^{\circ}: \boldsymbol{\Delta} \rightarrow$ $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ that reverses the ordering of the elements in each ordinal $[n] \in \boldsymbol{\Delta}$. In the notation of 1.1.1, the functor (-)° sends a face map $\delta^{i}:[n-1] \gtrdot[n]$ to the face map $\delta^{n-i}:[n-1] \succ[n]$ and sends the degeneracy map $\sigma^{i}:[n+1] \rightarrow[n]$ to the degeneracy map $\sigma^{n-i}:[n+1] \rightarrow[n]$. Precomposition with this involutive automorphism induces an involution (-) ${ }^{\mathrm{op}}: s \mathcal{S} e t \rightarrow s \mathcal{S} e t$ that sends a simplicial set $X$ to its opposite simplicial set $X^{\mathrm{op}}$, with the orientation of the vertices in each simplex reversed. This construction preserves all conical limits and colimits and induces an isomorphism $\left(Y^{X}\right)^{\mathrm{op}} \cong\left(Y^{\mathrm{op}}\right)^{X^{\mathrm{op}}}$ on exponentials.
nodes.statement_short: Reversing the order of ordinals induces an involution $X\mapsto X^{op}$ of simplicial sets, preserving limits and exponentials.

nodes.name: dual ∞-cosmos
nodes.statement: For any $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$, there is a dual $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{co}}$ with the same objects but with functor spaces defined by: $$ \operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{co}}}(A, B):=\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal{K}}(A, B)^{\mathrm{op}} . $$ The isofibrations, equivalences, and trivial fibrations in $\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{co}}$ coincide with those of $\mathcal{K}$.\\ Conical limits in $\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{c}^{\mathrm{o}}}$ coincide with those in $\mathcal{K}$, while the cotensor of $A \in \mathcal{K}$ with $U \in s \mathcal{S} e t$ is defined to be $A^{U^{\mathrm{op}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The dual ∞-cosmos $\mathcal{K}^{co}$ has opposite functor spaces, the same isofibrations, and cotensors by $U^{op}$.

nodes.name: discrete ∞-category
nodes.statement: 1.2.26. Definition (discrete $\infty$-categories). An $\infty$-category $E$ in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is discrete just when for all $X \in \mathcal{K}$ the functor space $\operatorname{Fun}(X, E)$ is a Kan complex.
differentia: for all $X \in \mathcal{K}$ the functor space $\operatorname{Fun}(X, E)$ is a Kan complex.

nodes.name: discrete ∞-categories in models
nodes.statement: In the $\infty$-cosmos of quasi-categories, the discrete $\infty$-categories are exactly the Kan complexes. Similarly, in the $\infty$-cosmoi of Example 1.2.24 whose $\infty$-categories are $(\infty, 1)$-categories in some model, the discrete $\boldsymbol{\infty}$-categories are the $\boldsymbol{\infty}$-groupoids.

nodes.name: internal characterization of discrete ∞-categories
nodes.statement: 1.2.27. Lemma. An $\infty$-category $E$ is discrete if and only if $E^{\mathbb{I}} \leadsto E^{2}$ is a trivial fibration.
conclusions: An $\infty$-category $E$ is discrete if and only if $E^{\mathbb{I}} \leadsto E^{2}$ is a trivial fibration.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.2.27
nodes.statement: Proof. By Definition 1.2.2, the isofibration $E^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow E^{2}$ is a trivial fibration if and only if for all $\infty$-categories $X$ the induced map on functor spaces $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Fun}\left(X, E^{\mathbb{I}}\right) & \longrightarrow \operatorname{Fun}\left(X, E^{2}\right) \\ \text { RII } & \text { RII } \\ \operatorname{Fun}(X, E)^{\mathbb{I}} & \longrightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(X, E)^{2} \end{aligned} $$ is a trivial fibration of quasi-categories. Via the universal property of the simplicial cotensor, Lemma 1.1.30 tells us that this map is a trivial fibration if and only if $\operatorname{Fun}(X, E)$ is a Kan complex.
nodes.statement_short: Representably reduce to $\mathrm{Fun}(X,E)^{\mathbb{I}}\to\mathrm{Fun}(X,E)^2$ and apply Lemma 1.1.30.

conclusions: the discrete $\infty$-categories in any $\infty$-cosmos assemble into an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}^{\sim}$.

nodes.name: cosmological functor
nodes.statement: 1.3.1. Definition (cosmological functor). A cosmological functor is a simplicial functor (see Definition A.2.6) between $\infty$-cosmoi that preserves the specified isofibrations and all of the cosmological limits.
differentia: preserves the specified isofibrations and all of the cosmological limits.

nodes.name: cosmological functors preserve equivalences
nodes.statement: 1.3.2. Lemma. Any cosmological functor also preserves equivalences and trivial fibrations.
conclusions: Any cosmological functor also preserves equivalences and trivial fibrations.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.3.2
nodes.statement: Proof. By Lemma 1.2.15 the equivalences in an $\infty$-cosmos coincide with the "homotopy equivalences" defined by cotensoring with the free-living isomorphism. Since a cosmological functor preserves simplicial cotensors, it preserves the data displayed in (1.2.16) and hence carries equivalences to equivalences. The preservation of trivial fibrations follows.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalences are homotopy equivalences via cotensors (Lemma 1.2.15), which cosmological functors preserve.

nodes.name: cosmological functors preserve discrete ∞-categories
nodes.statement: 1.3.3. Remark. Similarly, arguing from Definition 1.2.26 it would not be clear whether cosmological functors preserve discrete $\infty$-categories, but using the internal characterization of Lemma 1.2.27 - an $\infty$-category $A$ is discrete if and only if $A^{\mathbb{I}} \xrightarrow{ } A^{2}$ is a trivial fibration - this follows from the fact that cosmological functors preserve simplicial cotensors and trivial fibrations.
nodes.statement_short: Cosmological functors preserve discrete ∞-categories, by the internal characterization of Lemma 1.2.27.

nodes.name: examples of cosmological functors
nodes.statement: 1.3.4. Proposition. The following constructions define cosmological functors for any $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ : \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] The functor space $\operatorname{Fun}(X,-): \mathcal{K} \rightarrow Q$ Cat, for any $\infty$-category $X$. \item[(ii)] The underlying quasi-category functor $$ (-)_{0}:=\operatorname{Fun}(1,-): \mathcal{K} \rightarrow Q C a t, $$ specializing (i) to the terminal $\infty$-category 1. \item[(iii)] The simplicial cotensor $(-)^{U}: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$, for any simplicial set $U$. \item[(iv)] The exponential $(-)^{A}: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$, for any $\infty$-category $A$ in a cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$. \item[(v)] Pullback of isofibrations $f^{*}: \mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{/ A}$ along any functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$. \item[(vi)] Moreover, for any cosmological functor $F: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$ and any $\infty$-category $A \in \mathcal{K}$, the induced map on slices $F: \mathcal{K}_{/ A} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}_{/ F A}$ defines a cosmological functor. \end{itemize}
conclusions: The following constructions define cosmological functors for any $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ :
nodes.statement_short: Functor spaces, the underlying quasi-category, cotensors, exponentials, pullback along a functor and sliced cosmological functors are cosmological.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.3.4
nodes.statement: Proof. The first four of these statements are nearly immediate, the preservation of isofibrations being asserted explicitly as a hypothesis in each case and the preservation of limits following from familiar arguments. For (v), pullback in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is a simplicially enriched limit construction; one consequence of this is that $f^{*}: \mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{/ A}$ defines a simplicial functor. The action of the functor $f^{*}$ on a 0 -arrow\\ $g$ in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ is also defined by a pullback square: since the front and back squares in the displayed diagram are pullbacks the top square is as well\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-27_284_452_371_831}\\ Since isofibrations are stable under pullback, it follows that $f^{*}: \mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{/ A}$ preserves isofibrations. It remains to prove that this functor preserves the simplicial limits constructed in Proposition 1.2.22, which is fundamentally a consequence of the commutativity of limit constructions. In each case, this can be verified explicitly. We illustrate this computation for simplicial cotensors by constructing the commutative cube:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-27_392_678_914_727}\\ Since the front, back, and right faces are pullbacks, the left is as well.\\ The final statement (vi) is left as Exercise 1.3.i.
nodes.statement_short: (i)-(iv) nearly immediate; for (v) check preservation of isofibrations and limits by pullback-cube arguments; (vi) is Exercise 1.3.i.

nodes.name: Cat and Kan embed cosmologically in QCat
nodes.statement: 1.3.5. Example. By Propositions 1.2.11 and 1.2.12, the full subcategory inclusions Cat $\hookrightarrow$ QCat and Kan ↪ QCat both define cosmological functors (see also Lemma 6.1.4). These cosmological embeddings explicate the intuition that the formal category theory of 1-categories or of $\infty$-groupoids can be recovered as a special case of the formal category theory of $(\infty, 1)$-categories.

nodes.name: forgetful functor from the slice is not cosmological
nodes.statement: 1.3.6. Non-Example. The forgetful functor $\mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$ is simplicial and preserves isofibrations but does not define a cosmological functor, failing to preserve cotensors and products. However, by Proposition 1.3.4(v), its right adjoint $-\times B: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ does define a cosmological functor.

nodes.name: groupoid core is not cosmological
nodes.statement: 1.3.7. Non-Example. The cosmological embedding Kan →QCat has a right adjoint $(-)^{\sim}:$ QCat → Kan that carries each quasi-category to its " $\infty$-groupoid core" or maximal sub Kan complex, the simplicial subset containing those $n$-simplices whose edges are all isomorphisms. This core functor preserves isofibrations and 1-categorical limits but is not cosmological since it is not simplicially enriched: any functor $K \rightarrow Q$ whose domain is a Kan complex and whose codomain is a quasi-category factors through the inclusion $Q^{\simeq} \hookrightarrow Q$ via a unique map $K \rightarrow Q^{\simeq}$ but in general $\operatorname{Fun}(K, Q) \neq$ $\operatorname{Fun}\left(K, Q^{\simeq}\right)$, since a natural transformation $K \times \Delta[1] \rightarrow Q$ only factors through $Q^{\simeq} \hookrightarrow Q$ in the case where its components are invertible (see Lemma 12.1.12 however).

nodes.name: cosmological biequivalence
nodes.statement: 1.3.8. Definition (cosmological biequivalence). A cosmological functor defines a cosmological biequivalence $F: \mathcal{K} \leadsto \mathcal{L}$ if it additionally \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] is essentially surjective on objects up to equivalence: for all $C \in \mathcal{L}$ there exists $A \in \mathcal{K}$ so that $F A \simeq C$ and \item[(ii)] defines a local equivalence: for all $A, B \in \mathcal{K}$, the action of $F$ on functor spaces defines an equivalence of quasi-categories $$ \operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B) . $$ \end{itemize}
differentia: is essentially surjective on objects up to equivalence:

nodes.name: biequivalences between ∞-cosmoi of (∞,1)-categories
nodes.statement: 1.3.9. Example (biequivalences between $\infty$-cosmoi of $(\infty, 1)$-categories; §E.2). \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] The underlying quasi-category functors defined on the $\infty$-cosmoi of complete Segal spaces, Segal categories, and 1-complicial sets $$ \text { CSS } \xrightarrow[\sim]{(-)_{0}} \text { QCat } \quad \text { Segal } \xrightarrow[\sim]{(-)_{0}} \text { QCat } \quad 1-\text { Comp } \xrightarrow[\sim]{(-)_{0}} \text { QCat } $$ are all biequivalences. In the first two cases these are defined by "evaluating at the 0th row" and in the last case this is defined by "forgetting the markings." \item[(ii)] There are also cosmological biequivalences nerve: $Q$ Cat $\xrightarrow{\sim} C S \mathcal{S}$ and nerve: $Q$ Cat $\xrightarrow{\sim}$ Segal defined by Joyal and Tierney [64]. \item[(iii)] The functor disc: $C S S \bumpeq$ Segal defined by Bergner [14] that "discretizes" a complete Segal spaces also defines a cosmological biequivalence. \item[(iv)] Another cosmological biequivalence $(-)^{\natural}: Q$ Cat $\xrightarrow{\sim} 1-$ Comp that gives each quasi-category its "natural marking." \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Underlying quasi-category functors, Joyal–Tierney nerves, Bergner's discretization and the natural marking are cosmological biequivalences.

nodes.name: ∞-cosmos of (∞,1)-categories
nodes.statement: 1.3.10. Definition. An $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is an $\infty$-cosmos of $(\infty, 1)$-categories just when the underlying quasi-category $(-)_{0}: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow$ QCat is a cosmological biequivalence.

nodes.name: underlying quasi-category of internal homs
nodes.statement: 1.3.11. Remark. The underlying quasi-category functor $(-)_{0}: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow Q C$ at carries the internal homs of a cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ to the corresponding functor spaces: for any $\infty$-categories $A$ and $B$ in $\mathcal{K}$, we have $$ \left(B^{A}\right)_{0}:=\operatorname{Fun}\left(1, B^{A}\right) \cong \operatorname{Fun}(A, B) . $$ In the case where the $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is biequivalent to $Q$ Cat, we see in Chapters 10 and 11 that this entails no essential loss of categorical information.

nodes.name: cosmological biequivalences create equivalences
nodes.statement: 1.3.12. Lemma. Let $F: \mathcal{K} \xrightarrow{\boldsymbol{L}}$ be a cosmological biequivalence. Then: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] A functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ between $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ is an equivalence if and only if $F f: F A \rightarrow F B$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{L}$. \item[(ii)] A pair of $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ are equivalent if and only if their images in $\mathcal{L}$ are equivalent. \end{itemize}
also_stated_at: Cosmological biequivalences not only preserve equivalences but also reflect and create them.
conclusions: A functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ between $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ is an equivalence if and only if $F f: F A \rightarrow F B$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{L}$.
A pair of $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ are equivalent if and only if their images in $\mathcal{L}$ are equivalent.
A functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ between $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ is an equivalence if and only if $F f: F A \rightarrow F B$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{L}$.
A pair of $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ are equivalent if and only if their images in $\mathcal{L}$ are equivalent.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.3.12
nodes.statement: Proof. Lemma 1.3.2 implies that cosmological functors preserve equivalences and thus also the existence of an equivalence between a pair of $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$. To see that equivalences are also\\ reflected, suppose $f: A \rightarrow B$ is a functor in $\mathcal{K}$ with the property that $F f: F A \xrightarrow{\Rightarrow} F B$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{L}$. Now for any $\infty$-category $X$, simplicial functoriality provides a commutative diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-29_215_569_367_778}\\ so from the 2-of-3 property we conclude that $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ is an equivalence, proving that $f$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$. To see that equivalences are created, suppose now that $A$ and $B$ are $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ equipped with an equivalence:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-29_317_1231_820_449}\\ in $\mathcal{L}$. Since $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \xrightarrow{ } \operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B)$ and $\operatorname{Fun}(B, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(F B, F A)$ are equivalences of quasi-categories the induced functors between their homotopy categories $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)) \leadsto \mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B))$ and $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(B, A)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(F B, F A))$ are equivalences of categories, by Remark 1.1.24, and in particular essentially surjective. So we may lift $\tilde{f}$ and $\tilde{g}$ to functors $f: A \rightarrow B$ and $g: B \rightarrow A$ inh (Fun( $A, B)$ ) and $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(B, A))$, respectively, so that $F f \cong \widetilde{f}$ and $F g \cong \tilde{g}$. The commutative diagram of quasi-categories\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-29_194_828_1433_648}\\ induces a commutative diagram between their homotopy categories. In particular, by applying the composition bifunctor to the isomorphisms $F f \cong \tilde{f}$ and $F g \cong \tilde{g}$, we see that $$ F\left(\operatorname{id}_{A}\right)=\operatorname{id}_{F A} \cong \tilde{g} \circ \tilde{f} \cong F g \circ F f=F(g \circ f) $$ in h( $\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F A)$ ). By fully faithfulness of $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(A, A)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F A))$, this isomorphism lifts to an isomorphism $\mathrm{id}_{A} \cong g \circ f$ in $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(A, A))$. By Corollary 1.1.16, this isomorphism can be represented by a homotopy coherent isomorphism $\mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$, which internalizes to define a map $\alpha: A \rightarrow A^{\mathbb{I}}$ as required. The construction of the homotopy coherent isomorphism $\beta: B \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ from $f \circ g$ to $\operatorname{id}_{B}$ proceeds similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Preservation by Lemma 1.3.2, reflection by 2-of-3; creation by lifting inverses through homotopy categories of functor spaces.

nodes.name: slices of cosmological functors
nodes.statement: 1.3.i. Exercise. Prove that for any cosmological functor $F: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$ and any $A \in \mathcal{K}$, the induced map $F: \mathcal{K}_{/ A} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}_{/ F A}$ defines a cosmological functor.

nodes.statement: 1.3.ii. Exercise. Sketch a proof that cosmological biequivalences create equivalences between $\infty$-categor ies without passing to homotopy categories, by lifting and composing the homotopy coherent isomorphisms given as part of the data of the hypothesized equivalences.

nodes.name: 2-of-6 for cosmological biequivalences
nodes.statement: 1.3.iii. Exercise. Suppose $F: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}, G: \mathcal{L} \rightarrow \mathcal{M}$, and $H: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathcal{N}$ are cosmological functors, and assume that $G F$ and $H G$ are cosmological biequivalences. Show that $F, G, H$, and $H G F$ are cosmological biequivalences.

nodes.name: homotopy 2-category
nodes.statement: 1.4.1. Definition (homotopy 2-category). Let $\mathcal{K}$ be an $\infty$-cosmos. Its homotopy 2-category is the 2-category $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ whose \begin{itemize} \item[-] objects are the objects $A, B$ of $\mathcal{K}$, i.e., the $\infty$-categories; \item[-] 1-cells $f: A \rightarrow B$ are the 0-arrows in the functor space $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$, i.e., the $\infty$-functors; and \item[-] 2-cells $A \xrightarrow[g]{\underset{g}{f}} B$ are homotopy classes of 1-simplices in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$, which we call $\infty$-natural transformations. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h}\mathcal{K}$: ∞-categories, ∞-functors, and homotopy classes of 1-simplices in functor spaces as 2-cells.

nodes.name: hom-categories of the homotopy 2-category
nodes.statement: Put another way $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ is the 2-category with the same objects as $\mathcal{K}$ and with hom-categories defined by $$ \mathrm{hFun}(A, B):=\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)), $$ that is, $\mathrm{hFun}(A, B)$ is the homotopy category of the quasi-category $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$.

nodes.name: underlying category of a 2-category
nodes.statement: The underlying category of a 2-category is defined by simply forgetting its 2-cells.

nodes.name: change of base
nodes.statement: 1.4.2. Digression (change of base, §A.7). The homotopy category functor preserves finite products, as of course does its right adjoint. It follows that the adjunction of Proposition 1.1.11 induces a change-of-base adjunction\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-31_128_490_777_816}\\ whose left and right adjoints change the enrichment by applying the homotopy category functor or the nerve functor to the hom objects of the enriched category. Here 2-Cat and sSet-Cat can each be understood as 2-categories - of enriched categories, enriched functors, and enriched natural transformations - and both change of base constructions define 2-functors (see Propositions A.7.3 and A.7.5). Since the nerve embedding is fully faithful, 2-categories can be identified as a full subcategory comprised of those simplicial categories whose hom spaces are nerves of categories.
nodes.statement_short: The adjunction $h \dashv N$ preserves products, so it induces a change-of-base 2-adjunction between 2-categories and simplicial categories.

nodes.name: representing 2-cells in the homotopy 2-category
nodes.statement: 1.4.3. Lemma. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] Every 2-cell $A \underset{g}{\stackrel{\Downarrow}{g}} B$ in the homotopy 2-category of an $\infty$-cosmos is represented by a map of quasi-categories as below-left or equivalently by a functor as below-right\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-31_162_912_1556_605}\\ and two such maps represent the same 2 -cell if and only if they are homotopic as 1 -simplices in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$. \item[(ii)] Every invertible 2-cell $A \xrightarrow[g]{\cong} B$ in the homotopy 2-category of an $\infty$-cosmos is represented by a map of quasi-categories as below-left or equivalently by a functor as below-right\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-31_162_901_1995_612}\\ and two such maps represent the same invertible 2-cell if and only if their common restrictions along $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ are homotopic as 1 -simplices in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: Every 2-cell $A \underset{g}{\stackrel{\Downarrow}{g}} B$ in the homotopy 2-category of an $\infty$-cosmos is represented by a map of quasi-categories as below-left or equivalently by a functor as below-right

Every invertible 2-cell $A \xrightarrow[g]{\cong} B$ in the homotopy 2-category of an $\infty$-cosmos is represented by a map of quasi-categories as below-left or equivalently by a functor as below-right
nodes.statement_short: 2-cells in $\mathfrak{h}\mathcal{K}$ are represented by maps to $B^{2}$ and invertible ones by maps to $B^{\mathbb{I}}$, up to homotopy.

nodes.name: ∞-natural isomorphism
nodes.statement: Since the 2-cells in the homotopy 2-category are referred to as $\infty$-natural transformations, we refer to the invertible 2-cells in the homotopy 2-category as $\infty$-natural isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.4.3
nodes.statement: Proof. The statement (i) records the definition of the 2-cells in the homotopy 2-category and the universal property (1.2.7) of the simplicial cotensor. For (ii), a 2-cell in the homotopy 2-category is invertible if and only if it defines an isomorphism in the appropriate hom-category $\mathrm{hFun}(A, B)$. By Corollary 1.1.16 it follows that each invertible 2-cell $\alpha$ is represented by a homotopy coherent isomorphism $\alpha: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$, which similarly internalizes to define a functor ${ }^{「} \alpha^{\urcorner}: A \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$.
nodes.statement_short: (i) by definition and the cotensor universal property; (ii) invertible 2-cells are represented by homotopy coherent isomorphisms (Cor. 1.1.16).

nodes.name: simplicial functors induce 2-functors
nodes.statement: 1.4.4. Lemma. Any simplicial functor $F: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$ between $\infty$-cosmoi induces a 2 -functor $F: \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{L}$ between their homotopy 2-categories.
conclusions: induces a 2 -functor $F: \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{L}$ between their homotopy 2-categories.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.4.4
nodes.statement: Proof. The action of the induced 2-functor $F: \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{L}$ on objects and 1-cells is given by the corresponding action of $F: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$; recall an $\infty$-cosmos and its homotopy 2-category have the same underlying 1-category. Each 2-cell in $\mathfrak{h K}$ is represented by a 1-simplex in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$ which is mapped via\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-32_203_716_950_704}\\ to a 1-simplex representing a 2-cell in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{L}$. Since the action $F: \operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B)$ on functor spaces defines a morphism of simplicial sets, it preserves faces and degeneracies. In particular, homotopic 1-simplices in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$ are carried to homotopic 1-simplices in $\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B)$ so the action on 2-cells just described is well-defined. The 2-functoriality of these mappings follows from the simplicial functoriality of the original mapping.
nodes.statement_short: Act on 2-cells via 1-simplices of functor spaces; simplicial maps preserve homotopy of 1-simplices, so the action is well defined.

nodes.name: the terminal ∞-category is 2-terminal
nodes.statement: To illustrate, recall that the terminal $\infty$-category $1 \in \mathcal{K}$ has the universal property $\operatorname{Fun}(X, 1) \cong \mathbb{1}$ for all $X \in \mathcal{K}$. Applying the homotopy category functor we see that $1 \in \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ has the universal property $\mathrm{hFun}(X, 1) \cong \mathbb{1}$ for all $X \in \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$, which is expressed by saying that the $\infty$-category 1 defines a 2 -terminal object in the homotopy 2 -category. This 2-categorical universal property has both a 1-dimensional and a 2-dimensional aspect. Since $\mathrm{hFun}(X, 1) \cong \mathbb{1}$ is a category with a single object, there exists a unique morphism $X \rightarrow 1$ in $\mathcal{K}$, and since $\mathrm{hFun}(X, 1) \cong \mathbb{1}$ has only a single morphism, the only 2-cells in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ with codomain 1 are identities.
nodes.statement_short: Applying $h$ to $\mathrm{Fun}(X,1)\cong 1$ shows the terminal ∞-category is 2-terminal in the homotopy 2-category.

nodes.name: cartesian (closure)
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] The homotopy 2-category of any $\infty$-cosmos has 2-categorical products. \item[(ii)] The homotopy 2-category of a cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmos is cartesian closed as a 2-category. \end{itemize}
conclusions: The homotopy 2-category of any $\infty$-cosmos has 2-categorical products.
The homotopy 2-category of a cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmos is cartesian closed as a 2-category.
is cartesian closed as a 2-category.
