nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.4.5
nodes.statement: Proof. While the functor h: sSet → Cat only preserves finite products, the restricted functor h: QCat → Cat preserves all products on account of the simplified description of the homotopy category of a quasi-category given in Lemma 1.1.12. Thus for any set $I$ and family of $\infty$-categories $\left(A_{i}\right)_{i \in I}$ in $\mathcal{K}$, the homotopy category functor carries the isomorphism of functor spaces to an isomorphism of hom-categories $$ \operatorname{Fun}\left(X, \prod_{i \in I} A_{i}\right) \xrightarrow{\cong} \prod_{i \in I} \operatorname{Fun}\left(X, A_{i}\right) \quad \stackrel{\mathrm{h}}{\longrightarrow} \quad \mathrm{hFun}\left(X, \prod_{i \in I} A_{i}\right) \xrightarrow{\cong} \prod_{i \in I} \mathrm{hFun}\left(X, A_{i}\right) . $$ This proves that the homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ has products whose universal properties have both a 1-and 2-dimensional component, as described in the empty case for terminal objects above. If $\mathcal{K}$ is a cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmos, then for any triple of $\infty$-categories $A, B, C \in \mathcal{K}$ there exist exponential objects $C^{A}, C^{B} \in \mathcal{K}$ characterized by natural isomorphisms $$ \operatorname{Fun}(A \times B, C) \cong \operatorname{Fun}\left(A, C^{B}\right) \cong \operatorname{Fun}\left(B, C^{A}\right) . $$ Passing to homotopy categories we have natural isomorphisms $$ \mathrm{hFun}(A \times B, C) \cong \mathrm{hFun}\left(A, C^{B}\right) \cong \mathrm{hFun}\left(B, C^{A}\right), $$ which demonstrates that $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ is cartesian closed as a 2-category: functors $A \times B \rightarrow C$ transpose to define functors $A \rightarrow C^{B}$ and $B \rightarrow C^{A}$, and natural transformations transpose similarly.
nodes.statement_short: $h$ preserves all products of quasi-categories (Lemma 1.1.12), so functor-space isomorphisms pass to hom-categories, giving products and exponentials.

nodes.name: equivalence in a 2-category
nodes.statement: 1.4.6. Definition (equivalence). An equivalence in a 2-category is given by \begin{itemize} \item[-] a pair of objects $A$ and $B$; \item[-] a pair of 1-cells $f: A \rightarrow B$ and $g: B \rightarrow A$; and \item[-] a pair of invertible 2-cells\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-33_124_256_1210_605}\\ and\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-33_121_242_1179_1274} \end{itemize} When $A$ and $B$ are equivalent, we write $A \simeq B$ and refer to the 1-cells $f$ and $g$ as equivalences, denoted by "\~{}."

nodes.name: equivalences are equivalences
nodes.statement: 1.4.7. Theorem (equivalences are equivalences). In any $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$, the following are equivalent and characterize what it means for a functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ between $\infty$-categories to define an equivalence. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] For all $X \in \mathcal{K}$, the post-composition map $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ defines an equivalence of quasi-categories. \item[(ii)] There exists a functor $g: B \rightarrow A$ and natural isomorphisms $\alpha: \mathrm{id}_{A} \cong g f$ and $\beta: f g \cong \mathrm{id}_{B}$ in the homotopy 2-category. \item[(iii)] There exists a functor $g: B \rightarrow A$ and maps\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-33_312_245_2066_682}\\ and in the $\infty-\operatorname{cosmos} \mathcal{K}$.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-33_311_236_2067_1212} \end{itemize}
conclusions: the following are equivalent and characterize what it means for a functor $f: A \rightarrow B$ between $\infty$-categories to define an equivalence.
equivalent_conditions: For all $X \in \mathcal{K}$, the post-composition map $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ defines an equivalence of quasi-categories.
There exists a functor $g: B \rightarrow A$ and natural isomorphisms $\alpha: \mathrm{id}_{A} \cong g f$ and $\beta: f g \cong \mathrm{id}_{B}$ in the homotopy 2-category.
There exists a functor $g: B \rightarrow A$ and maps
nodes.statement_short: In an ∞-cosmos, representable equivalences, 2-categorical equivalences in $\mathfrak{h}\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathbb{I}$-homotopy equivalences coincide.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4.7
nodes.statement: Proof. For (i)⇒(ii), if the induced map $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ defines an equivalence of quasi-categories then the functor $f_{*}: \mathrm{hFun}(X, A) \leadsto \mathrm{hFun}(X, B)$ defines an equivalence of categories, by Remark 1.1.24. In particular, the equivalence $f_{*}: \operatorname{hFun}(B, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{hFun}(B, B)$ is essentially surjective so there exists $g \in \operatorname{hFun}(B, A)$ and an isomorphism $\beta: f g \cong \operatorname{id}_{B} \in \operatorname{hFun}(B, B)$. Now since $f_{*}: \operatorname{hFun}(A, A) \xrightarrow{\beth} \mathrm{hFun}(A, B)$ is fully faithful, the isomorphism $\beta f: f g f \cong f \in \mathrm{hFun}(A, B)$ can be lifted to define an isomorphism $\alpha^{-1}: g f \cong \operatorname{id}_{A} \in \operatorname{hFun}(A, A)$. This defines the data of a 2-categorical equivalence in Definition 1.4.6. To see that (ii)⇒(iii) recall from Lemma 1.4.3 that the natural isomorphisms $\alpha: \mathrm{id}_{A} \cong g f$ and $\beta: f g \cong \operatorname{id}_{B}$ in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ are represented by maps $\alpha: A \rightarrow A^{\mathbb{I}}$ and $\beta: B \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ in $\mathcal{K}$ as in (1.2.16). Finally, (iii)⇒(i) since $\operatorname{Fun}(X,-)$ carries the data of (iii) to the data of an equivalence of quasi-categories as in Definition 1.1.23.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications: (i)⇒(ii) via equivalences of hom-categories, (ii)⇒(iii) by Lemma 1.4.3, (iii)⇒(i) by applying $\mathrm{Fun}(X,-)$.

nodes.name: equivalence invariance of functor spaces
nodes.statement: 1.4.8. Corollary. Equivalences of $\infty$-categories $A^{\prime} \xrightarrow{\sim} A$ and $B \xrightarrow{ } B^{\prime}$ induce an equivalence of functor spaces $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}\left(A^{\prime}, B^{\prime}\right)$.
conclusions: induce an equivalence of functor spaces $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}\left(A^{\prime}, B^{\prime}\right)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.4.8
nodes.statement: Proof. The representable simplicial functors $\operatorname{Fun}(A,-): \mathcal{K} \rightarrow Q$ Cat and $\operatorname{Fun}(-, B): \mathcal{K}^{\text {op }} \rightarrow$ QCat induce 2-functors $\operatorname{Fun}(A,-): \mathfrak{h K} \rightarrow \mathfrak{h Q C a t}$ and $\operatorname{Fun}(-, B): \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{op}} \rightarrow \mathfrak{h Q C a t}$, which preserve the 2-categorical equivalences of Definition 1.4.6. By Theorem 1.4.7 this is what we wanted to show.
nodes.statement_short: Representable 2-functors preserve 2-categorical equivalences; conclude by Theorem 1.4.7.

nodes.name: isofibrations are isofibrations
nodes.statement: 1.4.9. Proposition (isofibrations are isofibrations). An isofibration $p: E \rightarrow B$ in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ also defines an isofibration in the homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h K}$ : given any invertible 2-cell as displayed below-left abutting to $B$ with a specified lift of one of its boundary 1-cells through $p$, there exists an invertible 2-cell abutting to $E$ with this boundary 1-cell as displayed below-right that whiskers with p to the original 2-cell.
assumptions: An isofibration $p: E \rightarrow B$ in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$
conclusions: also defines an isofibration in the homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h K}$ :

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.4.9
nodes.statement: Proof. The universal property of the statement says that the functor $$ p_{*}: \operatorname{hFun}(X, E) \rightarrow \operatorname{hFun}(X, B) $$ is an isofibration of categories in the sense defined in Proposition 1.2.11. By axiom 1.2.1(ii), since $p: E \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration in $\mathcal{K}$, the induced map $p_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, E) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ is an isofibration of quasi-categories. So it suffices to show that the functor $\mathrm{h}: Q$ Cat $\rightarrow$ Cat carries isofibrations of quasi-categories to isofibrations of categories. So let us now consider an isofibration $p: E \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories. By Corollary 1.1.16, every isomorphism $\beta$ in the homotopy category $\mathrm{h} B$ of the quasi-category $B$ is represented by a simplicial $\operatorname{map} \beta: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow B$. By Definition 1.1.17, the lifting problem\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-35_204_203_741_964}\\ can be solved, and the map $\gamma: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow E$ so produced represents a lift of the isomorphism from $\mathrm{h} B$ to an isomorphism in $\mathrm{h} E$ with domain $e$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing $h$ sends isofibrations of quasi-categories to isofibrations of categories; lift homotopy coherent isomorphisms.

nodes.name: isofibrations in homotopy 2-categories (convention)
nodes.statement: 1.4.10. Convention (on isofibrations in homotopy 2-categories). Since the converse to Proposition 1.4.9 does not hold, there is a potential ambiguity when using the term "isofibration" to refer to a map in the homotopy 2-category of an $\infty$-cosmos. We adopt the convention that when we declare a map in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ to be an isofibration we always mean this is the stronger sense of defining an isofibration in $\mathcal{K}$. This stronger condition gives us access to the 2-categorical lifting property of Proposition 1.4.9 and also to homotopical properties axiomatized in Definition 1.2.1, which ensure that the strictly defined limits of 1.2.1(i) are automatically equivalence invariant constructions (see §C. 1 and Proposition 6.2.8).

nodes.name: homotopy category of an ∞-category
nodes.statement: 1.4.11. Definition (homotopy category of an $\infty$-category). The homotopy category of an $\infty$-category $A$ in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is defined to be the homotopy category of its underlying quasi-category, that is: $$ \mathrm{h} A:=\mathrm{hFun}(1, A):=\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(1, A)) . $$

nodes.name: homotopy 2-category of Cat
nodes.statement: 1.4.i. Exercise. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] What is the homotopy 2-category of the $\infty$-cosmos Cat of 1-categories? \item[(ii)] Prove that the nerve defines a 2-functor $C a t \hookrightarrow \mathfrak{h} Q C a t$ that is locally fully faithful. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: homotopy 2-category of the dual ∞-cosmos
nodes.statement: 1.4.ii. Exercise. Demonstrate that the homotopy 2-category of the dual $\operatorname{cosmos} \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{co}}$ of an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is the co-dual of the homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ - in symbols $\mathfrak{h}\left(\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{O}}}\right) \cong(\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K})^{\text {co }}$ - with the domains and codomains of 2-cells but not 1-cells reversed (see Definition B.1.6).

nodes.name: natural isomorphisms and equivalences
nodes.statement: 1.4.iii. Exercise. Consider a natural isomorphism $A \xrightarrow[g]{f} B$ between a parallel pair of functors in an $\infty$-cosmos. Give two proofs that if either $f$ or $g$ is an equivalence then both functors are, either by arguing entirely in the homotopy 2-category or by appealing to Lemma 1.4.3.

nodes.name: characterizations of discrete objects
nodes.statement: 1.4.iv. Exercise. Extend Lemma 1.2.27 to show that the following four conditions are equivalent, characterizing the discrete objects $E$ in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ : \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $E$ is a discrete object in the homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$, that is, every 2-cell with codomain $E$ is invertible. \item[(ii)] For each $X \in \mathcal{K}$, the hom-category $\mathrm{hFun}(X, E)$ is a groupoid. \item[(iii)] For each $X \in \mathcal{K}$, the mapping quasi-category $\operatorname{Fun}(X, E)$ is a Kan complex. \item[(iv)] The isofibration $E^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow E^{2}$, induced by the inclusion of simplicial sets $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$, is a trivial fibration. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: cosmological biequivalences induce biequivalences
nodes.statement: 1.4.v. Exercise (10.3.1). Extend Lemma 1.4.4 to show that if $F: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$ is a cosmological biequivalence then $F: \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{L}$ is a 2-categorical biequivalence, a 2-functor that is essentially surjective on objects up to equivalence that locally defines an equivalence of hom-categories.

nodes.name: creation of equivalences revisited
nodes.statement: \href{http://1.4.vi}{1.4.vi}. Exercise. Let $F: \mathcal{K} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{L}$ be a cosmological biequivalence and let $A, B \in \mathcal{K}$. Re-prove part of the statement of Lemma 1.3.12: that if $F A \simeq F B$ in $\mathcal{L}$ then $A \simeq B$ in $\mathcal{K}$.

nodes.name: homotopy 2-category of a slice
nodes.statement: 1.4.vii. Exercise (3.6.2). Let $B$ be an $\infty$-category in the $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ and let $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ denote the 2-category whose \begin{itemize} \item[-] objects are isofibrations $E \rightarrow B$ in $\mathcal{K}$ with codomain $B$; \item[-] 1-cells are 1-cells in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ over $B$; and \end{itemize} \begin{center} \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-36_136_249_1455_938} \end{center} \begin{itemize} \item[-] 2-cells are 2-cells $\alpha$ in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-36_221_250_1661_937}\\ that lie over $B$ in the sense that $q \alpha=\mathrm{id}_{p}$. \end{itemize} Argue that the homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h}\left(\mathcal{K}_{/ B}\right)$ of the sliced $\infty$-cosmos has the same underlying 1-category but different 2-cells. How do these compare with the 2-cells of $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ ?

nodes.name: reduce to low dimensions
nodes.statement: Via the isomorphism $C \cong \operatorname{cosk}_{2} C$ from Remark 1.1.5 and the adjunction $\operatorname{sk}_{2} \dashv \operatorname{cosk}_{2}$ of C.5.2, the required lifting problem displayed below-left transposes to the one displayed below-right:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-03_203_1027_1504_548}\\ The functor $\mathrm{sk}_{2}$ replaces a simplicial set by its 2-skeleton, the simplicial subset generated by the simplices of dimension at most two. For $n \geq 4$, the inclusion $\operatorname{sk}_{2} \Lambda^{k}[n] \hookrightarrow \operatorname{sk}_{2} \Delta[n]$ is an isomorphism, in which case the lifting problems on the right admit (unique) solutions. So it remains only to solve the lifting problems on the left in the cases $n=2$ and $n=3$.
nodes.statement_short: Transpose along $sk_2\dashv cosk_2$; for $n\ge4$ the lifting is automatic, leaving $n=2,3$.

nodes.name: case n = 2
nodes.statement: To that end consider\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-03_196_1035_1991_544}\\ An inner horn $\Lambda^{1}[2] \rightarrow C$ defines a composable pair of arrows in $C$; an extension to a 2 -simplex exists precisely because any composable pair of arrows admits a (unique) composite.
nodes.statement_short: Inner 2-horns are filled by composites.

nodes.name: case n = 3
nodes.statement: An inner horn $\Lambda^{1}[3] \rightarrow C$ specifies the data of three composable arrows in $C$, as displayed in the following diagram, together with the composites $g f, h g$, and $(h g) f$.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-04_304_372_373_874}\\ Because composition is associative, the arrow $(h g) f$ is also the composite of $g f$ followed by $h$, which proves that the 2 -simplex opposite the vertex $c_{1}$ is present in $C$; by 2-coskeletality, the 3 -simplex filling this boundary sphere is also present in $C$. The filler for a horn $\Lambda^{2}[3] \rightarrow C$ is constructed similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Inner 3-horns are filled using associativity and 2-coskeletality.

nodes.name: construct the unit
nodes.statement: For any simplicial set $X$, there is a natural map from $X$ to the nerve of its homotopy category $\mathrm{h} X$; since nerves are 2 -coskeletal, it suffices to define the map $\mathrm{sk}_{2} X \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} X$, and this is given immediately by the construction of Definition 1.1.10.
nodes.statement_short: Define the unit $X\to hX$ on the 2-skeleton.

nodes.name: unit is an iso on nerves
nodes.statement: Note that the quotient map $X \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} X$ becomes an isomorphism upon applying the homotopy category functor and is already an isomorphism whenever $X$ is the nerve of a category.
nodes.statement_short: The quotient map is inverted by $h$ and invertible on nerves.

nodes.name: adjointness
nodes.statement: Thus the adjointness follows from Lemma B.4.2 or by direct verification of the triangle equalities.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by Lemma B.4.2.

nodes.name: groupoid implies Kan
nodes.statement: If the homotopy category of a quasi-category is a groupoid, then all of its 1-simplices are isomorphisms, and Proposition 1.1.14 then implies that all inner and outer horns have fillers. Thus, the quasi-category is a Kan complex.
nodes.statement_short: All arrows invertible, so Prop. 1.1.14 fills all horns.

nodes.name: Kan implies groupoid
nodes.statement: Conversely, in a Kan complex, all outer horns can be filled and in particular fillers for the horns displayed in Definition 1.1.13 can be used to construct left and right inverses for any 1-simplex, which can be rectified to a single two-sided inverse by Lemma 1.1.12.
nodes.statement_short: Outer horn fillers give left and right inverses.

nodes.name: land in the core
nodes.statement: If $f$ is an isomorphism, the map $f: 2 \rightarrow A$ lands in the maximal sub Kan complex contained in $A$ :\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-07_193_301_667_911}
nodes.statement_short: An isomorphism lands in the maximal sub Kan complex.

nodes.name: outer horn decomposition
nodes.statement: By Exercise 1.1.v, the inclusion 2 ↪ II can be expressed as a sequential composite of pushouts of outer horn inclusions.
nodes.statement_short: Exercise 1.1.v builds $\mathbb{I}$ from $2$ by outer horns.

nodes.name: extend in the Kan complex
nodes.statement: Since $A^{\simeq}$ is a Kan complex, this shows that the required extension exists and in fact lands in $A^{\simeq} \subset A$.
nodes.statement_short: A Kan complex fills these horns.

nodes.name: transpose the lifting property
nodes.statement: The lifting property that characterizes trivial fibrations transposes to another lifting property, displayed below-right\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-10_219_1186_702_469}\\ that asserts that $A$ admits extensions along maps formed by taking the Leibniz product - also known as the pushout product - of a simplex boundary inclusion $\partial \Delta[n] \hookrightarrow \Delta[n]$ with the inclusion $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transpose to extensions along Leibniz products with $2\hookrightarrow\mathbb{I}$.

nodes.name: decompose the Leibniz product
nodes.statement: By Exercise 1.1.v(ii) the inclusion $2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ is a sequential composite of pushouts of left outer horn inclusions. By Corollary D.3.11, a key step along the way to the proofs of Propositions 1.1.20 and 1.1.29, it follows that the Leibniz product is also a sequential composite of pushouts of left and inner horn inclusions.
nodes.statement_short: Exercise 1.1.v(ii) and Corollary D.3.11 decompose the Leibniz product into horn pushouts.

nodes.name: Kan implies trivial fibration
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a Kan complex, then the extensions displayed above right exist, and, by transposing, the map $A^{\mathbb{I}} \rightarrow A^{2}$ is a trivial fibration.
nodes.statement_short: A Kan complex has the extensions.

nodes.name: trivial fibration implies Kan
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $A^{\mathbb{I}} \xrightarrow{{ }^{2}}$ is a trivial fibration then in particular it is surjective on vertices. Thus every arrow in $A$ is an isomorphism, and Corollary 1.1.15 tells us that $A$ must be a Kan complex.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity on vertices makes every arrow invertible; apply Corollary 1.1.15.

nodes.name: simplicial enrichment
nodes.statement: The subcategory QCat $\subset$ sSet inherits its simplicial enrichment from the cartesian closed category of simplicial sets: by Proposition 1.1.20, whenever $A$ and $B$ are quasi-categories, $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B):=B^{A}$ is again a quasi-category.
nodes.statement_short: Functor spaces are quasi-categories by Prop. 1.1.20.

nodes.name: limits exist in sSet
nodes.statement: The cosmological limits postulated in 1.2.1(i) exist in the ambient category of simplicial sets. ${ }^{16}$ For instance, the defining universal property of the simplicial cotensor (1.2.7) is satisfied by the exponentials of simplicial sets. Moreover, since the category of simplicial sets is cartesian closed, each of the conical limits is simplicially enriched in the sense discussed in Digression 1.2.6 (see Exercise 1.2.ii and Proposition A.5.4).
nodes.statement_short: Cosmological limits exist and are enriched in sSet.

nodes.name: limits of quasi-categories
nodes.statement: We now argue that the full subcategory of quasi-categories inherits all these limit notions and at the same time establish the stability of the isofibrations under the formation of these limits. In fact, this latter property helps to prove the former. To see this, note that a simplicial set is a quasi-category if and only if the map from it to the point is an isofibration. More generally, if the codomain of any isofibration is a quasi-category then its domain must be as well. So if any of the maps in a limit cone over a diagram of quasi-categories are isofibrations, then it follows that the limit is itself a quasi-category.
nodes.statement_short: Limits along isofibrations of quasi-categories are quasi-categories.

nodes.name: isofibration axioms
nodes.statement: Since the isofibrations are characterized by a right lifting property, Lemma C.2.3 implies that the isofibrations contains all isomorphism and are closed under composition, product, pullback, and forming inverse limits of towers. In particular, the full subcategory of quasi-categories possesses these \footnotetext{${ }^{16}$ Any category of presheaves is cartesian closed, complete, and cocomplete - a "cosmos" in the sense of Bénabou. } limits. This verifies all of the axioms of 1.2.1(i) and 1.2.1(ii) except for the last two: Leibniz closure and closure under exponentiation $(-)^{X}$. These last closure properties are established in Proposition 1.1.20, and in fact by Exercise 1.1.vii, the former subsumes the latter . This completes the verification of the $\infty$-cosmos axioms.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma C.2.3 and Prop. 1.1.20 give the closure axioms.

nodes.name: equivalences coincide
nodes.statement: It remains to check that the equivalences and trivial fibrations coincide with those maps defined by 1.1.23 and 1.1.25. By Proposition 1.1.28 the latter coincidence follows from the former, so it remains only to show that the equivalences of 1.1.23 coincide with the representably defined equivalences: those maps of quasi-categories $f: A \rightarrow B$ for which $A^{X} \rightarrow B^{X}$ is an equivalence of quasi-categories in the sense of Definition 1.1.23. Taking $X=\Delta[0]$, we see immediately that representably defined equivalences are equivalences, and the converse holds since the exponential $(-)^{X}$ preserves the data defining a simplicial homotopy.
nodes.statement_short: Representable equivalences agree with Definition 1.1.23; trivial fibrations follow by Prop. 1.1.28.

nodes.name: completeness axiom
nodes.statement: It is well-known that the 2-category of categories is complete (and in fact also cocomplete) as a Cat-enriched category (see Definition A.6.17 or [67]). The categorically enriched category of categories becomes a quasi-categorically enriched category by applying the nerve functor to the homcategories (see §A.7). Since the nerve functor is a right adjoint, it follows formally that these 2-categorical limits become simplicially enriched limits. In particular, as proscribed in Proposition A.7.8, the cotensor of a category $A$ by a simplicial set $U$ is defined to be the functor category $A^{\text {hU }}$. This completes the verification of axiom (i).
nodes.statement_short: 2-categorical limits in Cat become simplicial limits via the nerve.

nodes.name: closure via lifting property
nodes.statement: Since the class of isofibrations is characterized by a right lifting property, Lemma C.2.3 implies that the isofibrations are closed under all of the limit constructions of 1.2.1(ii) except for the last two, and by Exercise 1.1.vii, the Leibniz closure subsumes the closure under exponentiation.
nodes.statement_short: Right lifting gives the closure properties except Leibniz ones.

nodes.name: Leibniz lifting problem
nodes.statement: To verify that isofibrations of categories $f: A \rightarrow B$ are stable under forming Leibniz cotensors with monomorphisms of simplicial sets $i: U \hookrightarrow V$, we must solve the lifting problem below-left\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-16_234_975_2081_575}\\ which transposes to the lifting problem above-right, which we can solve by hand. Here the map $\beta$ defines a natural isomorphism between $f s: \mathrm{h} V \rightarrow B$ and a second functor. Our task is to lift this\\ to a natural isomorphism $\gamma$ from $s$ to another functor that extends the natural isomorphism $\alpha$ along $\mathrm{h} i: \mathrm{h} U \rightarrow \mathrm{~h} V$. Note this functor hi need not be an inclusion, but it is injective on objects, which is enough.
nodes.statement_short: Transpose Leibniz stability to lifting a natural isomorphism along $hi$.

nodes.name: define the lift by cases
nodes.statement: We define the components of $\gamma$ by cases. If an object $v \in \mathrm{~h} V$ is equal to $i(u)$ for some $u \in \mathrm{~h} U$ define $\gamma_{i(u)}:=\alpha_{u}$; otherwise, use the fact that $f$ is an isofibration to define $\gamma_{v}$ to be any lift of the isomorphism $\beta_{v}$ to an isomorphism in $A$ with domain $s(v)$. The data of the map $\gamma: \mathrm{h} V \times \mathbb{I} \rightarrow A$ also entails the specification of the functor $\mathrm{h} V \rightarrow A$ that is the codomain of the natural isomorphism $\gamma$. On objects, this functor is given by $v \mapsto \operatorname{cod}\left(\gamma_{v}\right)$. On morphisms, this functor defined in the unique way that makes $\gamma$ into a natural transformation: $$ \left(k: v \rightarrow v^{\prime}\right) \mapsto \gamma_{v^{\prime}} \circ s(k) \circ \gamma_{v}^{-1} . $$
nodes.statement_short: Define $\gamma$ componentwise, extending $\alpha$ and lifting $\beta$ elsewhere.

nodes.name: identify equivalences
nodes.statement: This completes the proof that $C a t$ defines an $\infty$-cosmos. Since the nerve of a functor category, such as $A^{\mathbb{I}}$, is isomorphic to the exponential between their nerves, the equivalences of categories coincide with the equivalences of Definition 1.1.23. It follows that the equivalences in the $\infty$-cosmos of categories coincide with equivalences of categories, and since the surjective equivalences are the intersection of the equivalences and the isofibrations, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalences are equivalences of categories; trivial fibrations surjective equivalences.

nodes.name: isofibrations are Kan fibrations
nodes.statement: By Proposition 1.1.18, an isofibration between Kan complexes is a Kan fibration.
nodes.statement_short: Special outer horn lifting makes isofibrations Kan fibrations.

nodes.name: Kan fibrations are isofibrations
nodes.statement: Conversely, since the homotopy coherent isomorphism $\mathbb{I}$ can be built from the point $\mathbb{1}$ by attaching fillers to a sequence of outer horns, all Kan fibrations define isofibrations. This shows that between Kan complexes, isofibrations and Kan fibrations coincide.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{I}$ is built from outer horns, so Kan fibrations are isofibrations.

nodes.name: reduce to closure under limits
nodes.statement: So to show that the category of Kan complexes inherits an $\infty$-cosmos structure by restriction from the $\infty$-cosmos of quasi-categories, we need only verify that the full subcategory Kan ↪ QCat is closed under all of the limit constructions of axiom 1.2.1(i).
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to check closure of Kan under cosmological limits.

nodes.name: closure under limits
nodes.statement: For the conical limits, the argument mirrors the one given in the proof of Proposition 1.2.10, while the closure under cotensors is a consequence of Corollary D.3.11, which implies that the Kan complexes also define an exponential ideal in the category of simplicial sets.
nodes.statement_short: Conical limits as for QCat; cotensors by Corollary D.3.11.

nodes.name: remaining axiom
nodes.statement: The remaining axiom 1.2.1(ii) is inherited from the analogous properties established for quasi-categories in Proposition 1.2.10.
nodes.statement_short: Axiom (ii) is inherited from QCat.

nodes.name: functor spaces
nodes.statement: We prove these statements in the reverse order. By axiom 1.2.1(ii) and the definition of the trivial fibrations in an $\infty$-cosmos, we know that if $E \xrightarrow{ } B$ is a trivial fibration then $\operatorname{Fun}(X, E) \xrightarrow{\leadsto}$ $\operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ is both an isofibration and an equivalence, and hence by Proposition 1.1.28 a trivial fibration.
nodes.statement_short: Fun(X,-) of a trivial fibration is a trivial fibration by Prop. 1.1.28.

nodes.name: reduce to equivalences
nodes.statement: For stability under the remaining constructions, we know in each case that the maps in question are isofibrations in the $\infty$-cosmos; it remains to show only that the maps are also equivalences.
nodes.statement_short: The maps are isofibrations; it remains to show they are equivalences.

nodes.name: reduce to quasi-categories
nodes.statement: The equivalences in an $\infty$-cosmos are defined to be the maps that $\operatorname{Fun}(X,-)$ carries to equivalences of quasi-categories, so it suffices to verify that trivial fibrations of quasi-categories satisfy the corresponding stability properties.
nodes.statement_short: Representably reduce to trivial fibrations of quasi-categories.

nodes.name: quasi-categorical stability
nodes.statement: For the Leibniz stability properties, this is established in Proposition 1.1.29, while the remaining properties are covered by Lemma C.2.3.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 1.1.29 and Lemma C.2.3.

nodes.name: construct g and beta
nodes.statement: By hypothesis, if $f: A \rightarrow B$ defines an equivalence in the $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ then the induced map on post-composition $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(B, A) \xrightarrow{\sim \operatorname{Fun}(B, B) \text { is an equivalence of quasi-categories in the sense }}$ of Definition 1.1.23. Evaluating the inverse equivalence $\widetilde{g}: \operatorname{Fun}(B, B) \xrightarrow{\Rightarrow} \operatorname{Fun}(B, A)$ and homotopy $\widetilde{\beta}: \operatorname{Fun}(B, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)^{\mathbb{I}}$ at the 0-arrow $\operatorname{id}_{B} \in \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$, we obtain a 0-arrow $g: B \rightarrow A$ together with an isomorphism $\beta: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$ from the composite $f g$ to $\operatorname{id}_{B}$. By the defining universal property of the cotensor (1.2.7), this isomorphism internalizes to define the map $\beta: B \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ in $\mathcal{K}$ displayed on the right of (1.2.16).
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the inverse of $f_*$ at $\mathrm{id}_B$ to get $g$ and $\beta$.

nodes.name: construct alpha; converse
nodes.statement: Now the hypothesis that $f$ is an equivalence also provides an equivalence of quasi-categories $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$, and the map $\beta f: A \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ represents an isomorphism in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$ from $f g f$ to $f$. Since $f_{*}$ is an equivalence, we conclude from Remark 1.1.24 that $\mathrm{id}_{A}$ and $g f$ are isomorphic in\\ the quasi-category $\operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ : explicitly, such an isomorphism may be defined by applying the inverse equivalence $\tilde{h}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ and composing with the components at $\operatorname{id}_{A}, g f \in \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ of the isomorphism $\widetilde{\alpha}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, A) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)^{\mathbb{I}}$ from $\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Fun}(A, A)}$ to $\widetilde{h} f_{*}$. Now by Corollary 1.1.16 this isomorphism is represented by a map $\mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ from $\operatorname{id}_{A}$ to $g f$, which internalizes to a map $\alpha: A \rightarrow A^{\mathbb{I}}$ in $\mathcal{K}$ displayed on the left of (1.2.16). The converse is easy: the simplicial cotensor construction commutes with $\operatorname{Fun}(X,-)$, so a homotopy equivalence (1.2.16) induces a homotopy equivalence of quasi-categories as in Definition 1.1.23.
nodes.statement_short: Use Remark 1.1.24 and Cor. 1.1.16 to build $\alpha$; the converse applies Fun(X,-).

nodes.name: retracts
nodes.statement: Let $f: A \xrightarrow{口} B$ be an equivalence equipped with the data of (1.2.16) and consider a retract diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-19_267_389_1046_867}\\ By Lemma 1.2.15, to prove that $h: C \rightarrow D$ is an equivalence, it suffices to construct the data of an inverse homotopy equivalence. To that end define $k: D \rightarrow C$ to be the composite $v g s$ and then observe from the commutative diagrams\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-19_526_600_1496_427}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-19_518_584_1498_1107}\\ that $v^{\mathbb{I}} \alpha u: C \rightarrow C^{\mathbb{I}}$ and $t^{\mathbb{I}} \beta s: D \rightarrow D^{\mathbb{I}}$ define the required homotopy coherent isomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Build inverse-equivalence data for a retract from that of $f$.

nodes.name: 2-of-3 via isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Via Lemma 1.2.15, the 2-of-3 property for equivalences follows from the fact that the set of isomorphisms in a quasi-category is closed under composition. Homotopy coherent isomorphisms in a quasi-category represent isomorphisms in the homotopy category, whose composite in the homotopy category is then an isomorphism, which can be lifted to a representing homotopy coherent isomorphism by Corollary 1.1.16. ${ }^{17}$ We now apply this to the homotopy coherent isomorphisms in the functor spaces of an $\infty$-cosmos that form part of the data of an equivalence of $\infty$-categories.
nodes.statement_short: 2-of-3 reduces to composing isomorphisms in quasi-categories.

nodes.name: composition
nodes.statement: To prove that equivalences are closed under composition, consider a composable pair of equivalences with their inverse equivalences $$ A \underset{\stackrel{\sim}{k}}{\stackrel{f}{\rightleftarrows}} B \underset{\stackrel{\sim}{h}}{\stackrel{g}{\underset{\sim}{\sim}}} C $$ The equivalence data of Lemma 1.2.15 defines isomorphisms $\alpha: \operatorname{id}_{A} \cong k f \in \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$ and $\gamma: \operatorname{id}_{B} \cong$ $h g \in \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$, the latter of which whiskers to define $k \gamma f: k f \cong k h g f \in \operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$. Composing these, we obtain an isomorphism $\operatorname{id}_{A} \cong \operatorname{khg} f \in \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$, witnessing that $k h$ defines a left equivalence inverse of $g f$. The other isomorphism is constructed similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Whisker and compose the isomorphisms to invert $gf$.

nodes.name: right cancelation
nodes.statement: To prove that the equivalences are closed under right cancelation, consider a diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_203_358_747_882}\\ with $k$ an inverse equivalence to $f$ and $\ell$ and inverse equivalence to $g f$. We claim that $f \ell$ defines an inverse equivalence to $g$. One of the required isomorphisms $\mathrm{id}_{C} \cong g f \ell$ is given already. The other is obtained by composing three isomorphisms in $\operatorname{Fun}(B, B)$ $$ \operatorname{id}_{B} \xrightarrow[\bar{z}]{\beta^{-1}} f k \xrightarrow[\bar{z}]{f \delta k} f \ell g f k \xrightarrow[\bar{z}]{f \ell g \beta} f \ell g . $$
nodes.statement_short: Show $f\ell$ inverts $g$.

nodes.name: left cancelation
nodes.statement: The proof of stability of equivalence under left cancelation is dual.
nodes.statement_short: Left cancelation is dual.

nodes.name: functor spaces
nodes.statement: If $p: E \leadsto B$ is a trivial fibration, then by the final stability property of Lemma 1.2.14, so is $p_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, E) \xrightarrow{\Rightarrow} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ for any $\infty$-category $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1.2.14 makes $p_*$ a trivial fibration.

nodes.name: solve lifting problems
nodes.statement: By Definition 1.1.25, we may solve the lifting problem below-left\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_229_483_2221_483}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-20_225_552_2218_1088}\\ to find a map $s: B \rightarrow E$ so that $p s=\mathrm{id}_{B}$, and then solve the lifting problem above-right to construct the desired fibered homotopy. The converse is immediate from Lemma 1.2.15.
nodes.statement_short: Lift to a section and a fibered homotopy; converse by Lemma 1.2.15.

nodes.name: construct the factorization
nodes.statement: The displayed factorization is constructed by the pullback of an isofibration formed by the simplicial cotensor of the inclusion $\mathbb{1}+\mathbb{1} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{I}$ into the $\infty$-category $B$.\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-21_359_570_1018_780}\\ Note the map $q$ is a pullback of the trivial fibration $\mathrm{ev}_{0}: B^{\mathbb{I}} \xrightarrow{\text { ⇒ }} B$ and is hence a trivial fibration.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back the cotensor of $1+1\hookrightarrow\mathbb{I}$ into $B$; $q$ is a pullback of a trivial fibration.

nodes.name: section is an equivalence
nodes.statement: Its section $s$, constructed by applying the universal property of the pullback to the displayed cone with summit $A$, is thus an equivalence by the 2-of-3 property. Again by 2-of-3, it follows that $f$ is an equivalence if and only if $p$ is.
nodes.statement_short: By 2-of-3 the section is an equivalence, and $f$ is one iff $p$ is.

nodes.name: axioms from those of K
nodes.statement: The functor spaces are quasi-categories since axiom 1.2.1(ii) asserts that for any isofibration $q: F \rightarrow B$ in $\mathcal{K}$ the map $q_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(E, F) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(E, B)$ is an isofibration of quasi-categories. Other parts of this axiom imply that each of the limit constructions - such as the products and cotensors constructed in (iv) and (vi) - define isofibrations over $B$. The closure properties of the isofibrations in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ follow from the corresponding ones in $\mathcal{K}$. The most complicated of these is the Leibniz cotensor stability of the isofibrations in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$, which follows from the corresponding property in $\mathcal{K}$, since for a monomorphism of simplicial sets $i: X \hookrightarrow Y$ and an isofibration $r$ over $B$ as in (iii) above, the map $i \widehat{\Pi_{B}} r$ is constructed by pulling back $i \widehat{\pitchfork} r$ along $\Delta: B \rightarrow B^{Y}$.
nodes.statement_short: Functor spaces, limits and closure properties come from axiom 1.2.1(ii) in $\mathcal{K}$.

nodes.name: reduce to equivalences
nodes.statement: The fact that the above constructions define simplicially enriched limits in a simplicially enriched slice category are standard from enriched category theory. It remains only to verify that the equivalences in the $\infty$-cosmos of isofibrations are created by the forgetful functor $\mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show equivalences are created by the forgetful functor.

nodes.name: equivalence in K gives equivalence over B
nodes.statement: Suppose first that the map $f$ displayed in (vii) defines an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$. Then for any isofibration $s: A \rightarrow B$ the induced map on functor spaces in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ is defined by the pullback:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-23_268_952_517_585}\\ Since $f$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$, the map $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(A, E) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, F)$ is an equivalence, and so it follows that the induced map on fibers over $s$ is an equivalence as well.
nodes.statement_short: An equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$ induces equivalences on fibers of functor spaces.

nodes.name: converse
nodes.statement: For the converse implication, we appeal to Lemma 1.2.15. If $f: E \rightarrow F$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ then it admits a homotopy inverse in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$. The inverse equivalence $g: F \rightarrow E$ also defines an inverse equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$ and the required simplicial homotopies in $\mathcal{K}$ $$ E \xrightarrow{\alpha} \mathbb{I} \pitchfork_{B} p \longrightarrow E^{\mathbb{I}} \quad F \xrightarrow{\beta} \mathbb{I} \pitchfork_{B} q \rightarrow F^{\mathbb{I}} $$ are defined by composing with the top horizontal leg of the pullback defining the cotensor in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$.
nodes.statement_short: A homotopy inverse over $B$ is one in $\mathcal{K}$.

nodes.name: internal characterization
nodes.statement: By Lemma 1.2.15 the equivalences in an $\infty$-cosmos coincide with the "homotopy equivalences" defined by cotensoring with the free-living isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalences are homotopy equivalences (Lemma 1.2.15).

nodes.name: preserve equivalences
nodes.statement: Since a cosmological functor preserves simplicial cotensors, it preserves the data displayed in (1.2.16) and hence carries equivalences to equivalences. The preservation of trivial fibrations follows.
nodes.statement_short: Cotensors are preserved, hence equivalences and trivial fibrations.

nodes.name: parts (i)-(iv)
nodes.statement: The first four of these statements are nearly immediate, the preservation of isofibrations being asserted explicitly as a hypothesis in each case and the preservation of limits following from familiar arguments.
nodes.statement_short: (i)-(iv) are nearly immediate.

nodes.name: part (v)
nodes.statement: For (v), pullback in an $\infty$-cosmos $\mathcal{K}$ is a simplicially enriched limit construction; one consequence of this is that $f^{*}: \mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{/ A}$ defines a simplicial functor. The action of the functor $f^{*}$ on a 0 -arrow\\ $g$ in $\mathcal{K}_{/ B}$ is also defined by a pullback square: since the front and back squares in the displayed diagram are pullbacks the top square is as well\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-27_284_452_371_831}\\ Since isofibrations are stable under pullback, it follows that $f^{*}: \mathcal{K}_{/ B} \rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{/ A}$ preserves isofibrations. It remains to prove that this functor preserves the simplicial limits constructed in Proposition 1.2.22, which is fundamentally a consequence of the commutativity of limit constructions. In each case, this can be verified explicitly. We illustrate this computation for simplicial cotensors by constructing the commutative cube:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-27_392_678_914_727}\\ Since the front, back, and right faces are pullbacks, the left is as well.
nodes.statement_short: Pullback preserves isofibrations and, by cube arguments, cosmological limits.

nodes.name: part (vi)
nodes.statement: The final statement (vi) is left as Exercise 1.3.i.
nodes.statement_short: (vi) is Exercise 1.3.i.

nodes.name: preservation
nodes.statement: Lemma 1.3.2 implies that cosmological functors preserve equivalences and thus also the existence of an equivalence between a pair of $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$.
nodes.statement_short: Preservation by Lemma 1.3.2.

nodes.name: reflection
nodes.statement: To see that equivalences are also\\ reflected, suppose $f: A \rightarrow B$ is a functor in $\mathcal{K}$ with the property that $F f: F A \xrightarrow{\Rightarrow} F B$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{L}$. Now for any $\infty$-category $X$, simplicial functoriality provides a commutative diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-29_215_569_367_778}\\ so from the 2-of-3 property we conclude that $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ is an equivalence, proving that $f$ is an equivalence in $\mathcal{K}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reflection by local equivalence and 2-of-3.

nodes.name: creation
nodes.statement: To see that equivalences are created, suppose now that $A$ and $B$ are $\infty$-categories in $\mathcal{K}$ equipped with an equivalence:\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-29_317_1231_820_449}\\ in $\mathcal{L}$. Since $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \xrightarrow{ } \operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B)$ and $\operatorname{Fun}(B, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(F B, F A)$ are equivalences of quasi-categories the induced functors between their homotopy categories $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)) \leadsto \mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B))$ and $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(B, A)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(F B, F A))$ are equivalences of categories, by Remark 1.1.24, and in particular essentially surjective. So we may lift $\tilde{f}$ and $\tilde{g}$ to functors $f: A \rightarrow B$ and $g: B \rightarrow A$ inh (Fun( $A, B)$ ) and $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(B, A))$, respectively, so that $F f \cong \widetilde{f}$ and $F g \cong \tilde{g}$. The commutative diagram of quasi-categories\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-29_194_828_1433_648}\\ induces a commutative diagram between their homotopy categories. In particular, by applying the composition bifunctor to the isomorphisms $F f \cong \tilde{f}$ and $F g \cong \tilde{g}$, we see that $$ F\left(\operatorname{id}_{A}\right)=\operatorname{id}_{F A} \cong \tilde{g} \circ \tilde{f} \cong F g \circ F f=F(g \circ f) $$ in h( $\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F A)$ ). By fully faithfulness of $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(A, A)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F A))$, this isomorphism lifts to an isomorphism $\mathrm{id}_{A} \cong g \circ f$ in $\mathrm{h}(\operatorname{Fun}(A, A))$. By Corollary 1.1.16, this isomorphism can be represented by a homotopy coherent isomorphism $\mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, A)$, which internalizes to define a map $\alpha: A \rightarrow A^{\mathbb{I}}$ as required. The construction of the homotopy coherent isomorphism $\beta: B \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ from $f \circ g$ to $\operatorname{id}_{B}$ proceeds similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Lift inverse and isomorphisms through equivalences of homotopy categories of functor spaces.

nodes.name: part (i)
nodes.statement: The statement (i) records the definition of the 2-cells in the homotopy 2-category and the universal property (1.2.7) of the simplicial cotensor.
nodes.statement_short: (i) is the definition plus the cotensor property.

nodes.name: part (ii)
nodes.statement: For (ii), a 2-cell in the homotopy 2-category is invertible if and only if it defines an isomorphism in the appropriate hom-category $\mathrm{hFun}(A, B)$. By Corollary 1.1.16 it follows that each invertible 2-cell $\alpha$ is represented by a homotopy coherent isomorphism $\alpha: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$, which similarly internalizes to define a functor ${ }^{「} \alpha^{\urcorner}: A \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$.
nodes.statement_short: (ii) invertible 2-cells are homotopy coherent isomorphisms (Cor. 1.1.16).

nodes.name: objects and 1-cells
nodes.statement: The action of the induced 2-functor $F: \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathfrak{h} \mathcal{L}$ on objects and 1-cells is given by the corresponding action of $F: \mathcal{K} \rightarrow \mathcal{L}$; recall an $\infty$-cosmos and its homotopy 2-category have the same underlying 1-category.
nodes.statement_short: On objects and 1-cells use $F$ itself.

nodes.name: 2-cells
nodes.statement: Each 2-cell in $\mathfrak{h K}$ is represented by a 1-simplex in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$ which is mapped via\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-32_203_716_950_704}\\ to a 1-simplex representing a 2-cell in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{L}$.
nodes.statement_short: Map representing 1-simplices of functor spaces.

nodes.name: well-defined
nodes.statement: Since the action $F: \operatorname{Fun}(A, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B)$ on functor spaces defines a morphism of simplicial sets, it preserves faces and degeneracies. In particular, homotopic 1-simplices in $\operatorname{Fun}(A, B)$ are carried to homotopic 1-simplices in $\operatorname{Fun}(F A, F B)$ so the action on 2-cells just described is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: Simplicial maps preserve homotopies of 1-simplices.

nodes.name: 2-functoriality
nodes.statement: The 2-functoriality of these mappings follows from the simplicial functoriality of the original mapping.
nodes.statement_short: 2-functoriality from simplicial functoriality.

nodes.name: products
nodes.statement: While the functor h: sSet → Cat only preserves finite products, the restricted functor h: QCat → Cat preserves all products on account of the simplified description of the homotopy category of a quasi-category given in Lemma 1.1.12. Thus for any set $I$ and family of $\infty$-categories $\left(A_{i}\right)_{i \in I}$ in $\mathcal{K}$, the homotopy category functor carries the isomorphism of functor spaces to an isomorphism of hom-categories $$ \operatorname{Fun}\left(X, \prod_{i \in I} A_{i}\right) \xrightarrow{\cong} \prod_{i \in I} \operatorname{Fun}\left(X, A_{i}\right) \quad \stackrel{\mathrm{h}}{\longrightarrow} \quad \mathrm{hFun}\left(X, \prod_{i \in I} A_{i}\right) \xrightarrow{\cong} \prod_{i \in I} \mathrm{hFun}\left(X, A_{i}\right) . $$ This proves that the homotopy 2-category $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ has products whose universal properties have both a 1-and 2-dimensional component, as described in the empty case for terminal objects above.
nodes.statement_short: $h$ preserves products of quasi-categories, so $\mathfrak{h}\mathcal{K}$ has 2-products.

nodes.name: cartesian closure
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{K}$ is a cartesian closed $\infty$-cosmos, then for any triple of $\infty$-categories $A, B, C \in \mathcal{K}$ there exist exponential objects $C^{A}, C^{B} \in \mathcal{K}$ characterized by natural isomorphisms $$ \operatorname{Fun}(A \times B, C) \cong \operatorname{Fun}\left(A, C^{B}\right) \cong \operatorname{Fun}\left(B, C^{A}\right) . $$ Passing to homotopy categories we have natural isomorphisms $$ \mathrm{hFun}(A \times B, C) \cong \mathrm{hFun}\left(A, C^{B}\right) \cong \mathrm{hFun}\left(B, C^{A}\right), $$ which demonstrates that $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ is cartesian closed as a 2-category: functors $A \times B \rightarrow C$ transpose to define functors $A \rightarrow C^{B}$ and $B \rightarrow C^{A}$, and natural transformations transpose similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Passing exponential isomorphisms to homotopy categories gives cartesian closure.

nodes.name: (i)⇒(ii)
nodes.statement: For (i)⇒(ii), if the induced map $f_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ defines an equivalence of quasi-categories then the functor $f_{*}: \mathrm{hFun}(X, A) \leadsto \mathrm{hFun}(X, B)$ defines an equivalence of categories, by Remark 1.1.24. In particular, the equivalence $f_{*}: \operatorname{hFun}(B, A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{hFun}(B, B)$ is essentially surjective so there exists $g \in \operatorname{hFun}(B, A)$ and an isomorphism $\beta: f g \cong \operatorname{id}_{B} \in \operatorname{hFun}(B, B)$. Now since $f_{*}: \operatorname{hFun}(A, A) \xrightarrow{\beth} \mathrm{hFun}(A, B)$ is fully faithful, the isomorphism $\beta f: f g f \cong f \in \mathrm{hFun}(A, B)$ can be lifted to define an isomorphism $\alpha^{-1}: g f \cong \operatorname{id}_{A} \in \operatorname{hFun}(A, A)$. This defines the data of a 2-categorical equivalence in Definition 1.4.6.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalences of hom-categories give $g$, $\beta$ and then $\alpha$.

nodes.name: (ii)⇒(iii)
nodes.statement: To see that (ii)⇒(iii) recall from Lemma 1.4.3 that the natural isomorphisms $\alpha: \mathrm{id}_{A} \cong g f$ and $\beta: f g \cong \operatorname{id}_{B}$ in $\mathfrak{h} \mathcal{K}$ are represented by maps $\alpha: A \rightarrow A^{\mathbb{I}}$ and $\beta: B \rightarrow B^{\mathbb{I}}$ in $\mathcal{K}$ as in (1.2.16).
nodes.statement_short: Represent the isomorphisms by Lemma 1.4.3.

nodes.name: (iii)⇒(i)
nodes.statement: Finally, (iii)⇒(i) since $\operatorname{Fun}(X,-)$ carries the data of (iii) to the data of an equivalence of quasi-categories as in Definition 1.1.23.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Fun(X,-).

nodes.name: reformulate
nodes.statement: The universal property of the statement says that the functor $$ p_{*}: \operatorname{hFun}(X, E) \rightarrow \operatorname{hFun}(X, B) $$ is an isofibration of categories in the sense defined in Proposition 1.2.11.
nodes.statement_short: Restate as $p_*$ on hom-categories being an isofibration of categories.

nodes.name: axiom 1.2.1(ii)
nodes.statement: By axiom 1.2.1(ii), since $p: E \rightarrow B$ is an isofibration in $\mathcal{K}$, the induced map $p_{*}: \operatorname{Fun}(X, E) \rightarrow \operatorname{Fun}(X, B)$ is an isofibration of quasi-categories.
nodes.statement_short: $p_*$ is an isofibration of quasi-categories.

nodes.name: reduce to quasi-categories
nodes.statement: So it suffices to show that the functor $\mathrm{h}: Q$ Cat $\rightarrow$ Cat carries isofibrations of quasi-categories to isofibrations of categories.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that $h$ preserves isofibrations.

nodes.name: represent isomorphisms
nodes.statement: So let us now consider an isofibration $p: E \rightarrow B$ between quasi-categories. By Corollary 1.1.16, every isomorphism $\beta$ in the homotopy category $\mathrm{h} B$ of the quasi-category $B$ is represented by a simplicial $\operatorname{map} \beta: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow B$.
nodes.statement_short: Represent an isomorphism in $hB$ by $\mathbb{I}\to B$ (Cor. 1.1.16).

nodes.name: lift
nodes.statement: By Definition 1.1.17, the lifting problem\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{b375083c-8174-49a1-a017-e977744038d8-35_204_203_741_964}\\ can be solved, and the map $\gamma: \mathbb{I} \rightarrow E$ so produced represents a lift of the isomorphism from $\mathrm{h} B$ to an isomorphism in $\mathrm{h} E$ with domain $e$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift by the isofibration property.
